blocks.subject: lemma:G0005
blocks.title: Father, in Jesus' own language
blocks.body:
*Abba* is an Aramaic word for "father", carried untranslated into the Greek New Testament. It occurs three times, and each time it is immediately followed by the Greek *ho patēr*, "the Father": Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36) and believers crying out by the Spirit (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6).

It is the form of address a child, young or grown, used to a father in the home. The New Testament keeps the Aramaic sound because it was remembered as Jesus' own way of praying, and the earliest Greek-speaking churches went on using it.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0005
blocks.body:
In Second Temple Judaism God could be called Father (Isa 63:16; Jer 3:19; Sir 23:1), but usually of Israel as a people and in formal prayer language. Jesus' habit of addressing God simply as *Abba* in personal prayer stands out in the Gospel tradition.

Paul writes to Greek-speaking churches in Rome and Galatia, yet assumes they know the Aramaic word. That suggests *Abba* had already become part of shared Christian prayer, probably linked with the Lord's Prayer ("Father", Luke 11:2) and with baptism, where believers received the Spirit of the Son (Gal 4:6).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0005
blocks.body:
There is no Septuagint background, since *abba* is Aramaic, not Hebrew. The Greek New Testament transliterates it and adds a translation: *Abba ho patēr*.

The Latin Vulgate keeps the same pattern: *Abba, Pater*. Tyndale and the King James Version print "Abba, Father", and nearly every modern English version does the same, so readers still hear the original word beside its meaning. A few paraphrases render it "Papa" or "Dear Father" to bring out its warmth.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0005
blocks.title: Does abba mean Daddy?
blocks.body:
A popular claim says *abba* means "Daddy", a toddler's word. That has been widely challenged. *Abba* was used by adult children as well as small ones, and it carries both intimacy and respect, closer to "Father" spoken at home than to baby-talk.

Two things are agreed: the word is family language rather than court language, and its use by Jesus in prayer was striking. The disagreement is only over how childlike the register is. The safest reading holds both tenderness and trust, as in Gethsemane, where *Abba* comes with "not what I will, but what you will" (Mark 14:36).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0005
blocks.title: Sharing the Son's prayer
blocks.body:
*Abba* is the heart of the relational gospel in one word. Jesus did not merely teach that God is like a father; He lived inside that relationship and prayed out of it, even in agony (Mark 14:36).

The astonishing thing is that Paul says the same cry now rises in us. "God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father!" (Gal 4:6). We are not given a new religion of rules but brought into the Son's own place before the Father. Adoption (Rom 8:15) is not a legal fiction; it is sharing the Son's prayer life.

If Jesus is perfect theology, then the God we meet in Scripture is first of all *Abba*: the Father who is fully revealed in the Son (John 14:9).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0932
blocks.title: God's reign, not a place in the sky
blocks.body:
*Basileia* means "kingship, royal rule, reign" and, by extension, the realm ruled. In the New Testament (161 times) it is mostly dynamic: not a territory on a map but God's active reign breaking in. Jesus' first proclamation is "the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God has come near" (Mark 1:15).

Matthew usually says "kingdom of heaven", a reverent Jewish way of saying "kingdom of God" that avoids overusing the divine name. It does not mean a kingdom located in the sky. Jesus speaks of it as present (Luke 11:20; 17:21) and as still growing towards fullness (Matt 13:31-33).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0932
blocks.body:
Jesus' hearers knew Daniel's vision of a kingdom "set up by the God of heaven" that would never be destroyed and would fill the earth (Dan 2:44; 7:14, 27). Many Second Temple Jews hoped for a Davidic king who would drive out the Gentiles and restore Israel (Psalms of Solomon 17).

They also lived under Rome. Greek-speaking subjects called the emperor *basileus*, "king" (John 19:15; 1 Pet 2:17). To announce another *basileia* was therefore politically charged. Jesus redefined it: a kingdom not from this world in its source (John 18:36), advancing by healing, forgiveness and self-giving love rather than the sword.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0932
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *basileia* translates Hebrew *malkut* and *mamlakah*, "kingdom, reign" (e.g. Ps 145:13, "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom"). Aramaic *malku* in Daniel stands behind Jesus' own usage.

The Vulgate uses *regnum*, which can mean both "reign" and "realm". English "kingdom" (Tyndale, KJV and most modern versions) leans towards the realm sense, which has encouraged readers to think of a place you go to. Some scholars and versions prefer "reign" or "rule of God" in places like Mark 1:15 to recover the active sense.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0932
blocks.title: A growing kingdom
blocks.body:
The kingdom is what life looks like when the Father has His way. Jesus shows it: lepers touched, debts released, enemies loved, tables opened to sinners. Where the King is, the kingdom is (Luke 17:21).

Jesus' parables picture growth: a mustard seed becoming a tree, leaven working through the whole lump (Matt 13:31-33), a stone becoming a mountain that fills the earth (Dan 2:35). This supports a hopeful, postmillennial reading: Christ already reigns (Matt 28:18; 1 Cor 15:25), and His kingdom spreads through history by the gospel until the nations are discipled.

Entering the kingdom is not first about escaping earth but being born into the Father's family (John 3:3, 5) and joining His project of setting the world right.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0932
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads Jesus' kingdom announcement within Israel's story: Jesus presented Himself as the one through whom Israel's God was at last returning to Zion to reign, though in a way that overturned expectations of violent liberation. The kingdom came through Jesus' own vocation, culminating in the cross. This reading ties the kingdom closely to Jesus' own person and death: the kingdom is not an abstract idea He taught but the reign of God arriving in Him. It has been influential, though many scholars question parts of the 'return from exile' framework.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on the kingdom of God and the return of YHWH to Zion)

blocks.subject: lemma:G0932
blocks.body: Keith Mathison argues from the growth parables of Matt 13 and from Old Testament prophecies of worldwide blessing that Christ's kingdom, inaugurated at His first coming, will grow until the gospel has transformed the nations before His return. This is the postmillennial hope. Postmillennialists such as Mathison see this growth as gradual and gospel-driven rather than imposed by force. Most Christians today hold amillennial or premillennial views instead, so this remains a minority position, though one with a long Reformed history.

citations.ref: Postmillennialism: An Eschatology of Hope (on the kingdom parables)

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.title: A change of mind and direction
blocks.body:
*Metanoeō* (34 times) combines *meta* ("after, change") and *noeō* ("perceive, think"). In ordinary Greek it means "to change one's mind" or "to think again", often with regret. In the New Testament it means a turning of the whole person: a new way of seeing that leads to a new way of living (Luke 3:8-14).

It opens the preaching of John (Matt 3:2), Jesus (Mark 1:15) and the apostles (Acts 2:38). In Jesus' summary it is joined to trust: "repent and believe in the gospel". The change of mind is a response to good news, not a payment for it.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.body:
The Hebrew Scriptures mostly speak of repentance as *shuv*, "to turn back, return" to God (Jer 3:12-14; Hos 14:1). Jesus' call to "repent" in Galilee would have sounded like the prophets' call to return.

There is also a political edge. The Jewish historian Josephus describes telling a rebel leader to "repent and be loyal to me", meaning abandon his own plans and trust Josephus instead. Some scholars hear something similar in Jesus' call: turn from Israel's way of violent revolution and trust Him and His way of being God's people.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *metanoeō* is uncommon and usually renders Hebrew *nicham*, "to relent, be sorry" (e.g. Jer 18:8; Joel 2:13-14), while *shuv* is usually *epistrephō*, "to turn".

The Latin Vulgate rendered *metanoeite* as *paenitentiam agite*, "do penance" (Matt 3:2; 4:17), which medieval readers linked with the sacrament of penance. Erasmus in his notes on Matt 3:2 suggested *resipiscite*, "come to your senses". Tyndale chose "repent" instead of "do penance", a choice Thomas More attacked; the KJV and modern versions follow Tyndale.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.body:
**How the penitential reading arose.** Once *metanoeō* became *paenitentiam agite*, repentance in the Latin West was increasingly understood as a sequence of acts: contrition, confession to a priest and satisfaction (works that paid the temporal penalty of sin). Indulgences grew out of this system.

Luther's first thesis of 1517 turned back to the Greek sense: the whole life of believers is to be repentance, not a single sacramental act. Calvin later defined repentance as a true turning of our life to God.

The relational reading goes further: repentance is not a payment that buys forgiveness but the turn home in response to a Father already running (Luke 15:17-20).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.title: Waking up to the Father
blocks.body:
Repentance is changing your mind about God because of Jesus. The younger son in Luke 15 "came to himself" and turned home with a speech about earning his way back as a hired servant. The father's embrace interrupted the speech (Luke 15:20-22). That is the shape of *metanoia*: the goodness of God leads us to it (Rom 2:4).

So repentance is not grovelling to change God's attitude; it is waking up to the Father's attitude, already shown in the Son. "The kingdom has come near; repent and believe" means: reality has changed, so change your thinking and trust the good news.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.body: Athanasius argued that repentance alone could not heal humanity, because it stops wrongdoing but does not recall human nature from the corruption into which it had fallen. That required the Word Himself to take a body and renew humanity from within. Repentance is the right response, but the cure is union with the incarnate Word. This places repentance inside a larger healing story. Turning back matters, but the decisive change happens in Christ, who takes our nature, dies our death and raises it to life. Repentance is our awakening to and welcome of what He has done.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3340
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads Jesus' call to repent as having a concrete first-century sense: Israel was to abandon its agenda of armed resistance against Rome and follow Jesus' way of being God's people. He points to the parallel phrase in Josephus. The personal sense of turning from sin is included, but the call was also national and political.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on repentance and belief)

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.title: Of the age
blocks.body:
*Aiōnios* (71 times) is the adjective from *aiōn*, "age". Its basic sense is "belonging to the age". Depending on context it means "long-lasting", "everlasting", or "of the age to come".

It describes God Himself (Rom 16:26), the Spirit (Heb 9:14), and the covenant (Heb 13:20), where "everlasting" fits. Its most frequent use is in "*zōē aiōnios*", "eternal life" (John 3:16; 17:3), which echoes Daniel's "life of the age" for those raised (Dan 12:2). Here the word speaks as much about the quality and source of the life (the life of God's new age) as about its length.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.body:
Jewish thought in Jesus' day divided history into "this age" and "the age to come" (Matt 12:32). Later rabbinic texts speak of "the life of the world to come" (*chayyei ha-olam ha-ba*). When a man asked Jesus how to inherit *zōē aiōnios* (Mark 10:17), he meant: how do I share in the life of the coming age when God renews the world?

In Greek writers *aiōnios* could mean "lasting for an age" or "perpetual". Plato used it for the timeless realm, which later fed Christian ideas of eternity as timelessness.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *aiōnios* mostly renders Hebrew *olam*, "long duration, antiquity, futurity", e.g. "an everlasting covenant" (Gen 17:7) and "everlasting life" (Dan 12:2). *Olam* itself can describe things that end, such as a slave serving "for ever" (Exod 21:6).

Jerome's Vulgate translated *aiōnios* as *aeternus* or *sempiternus*, words that in Latin theology meant unending or timeless. The KJV used "eternal" and "everlasting" interchangeably, even within one verse (Matt 25:46). Some modern translations, mostly from universalist writers, try "age-long" or "of the Age" to recover the link with *aiōn*.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.title: Eternal punishment and eternal life
blocks.body:
**Does *aiōnios* mean "unending" in Matt 25:46?** Jesus speaks of *kolasis aiōnios* and *zōē aiōnios* in the same breath.

- *Majority view:* the word must mean the same in both halves, so if the life is unending, the punishment is too.
- *Minority view (some Fathers and modern universalists):* *aiōnios* describes the age the punishment and life belong to, not their length; it qualifies the source (God's coming age), so the punishment may be corrective and finite.
- *Conditional immortality:* the result (destruction) is permanent, not the experience of it.

The word alone cannot settle the question; each view appeals to wider themes in Scripture.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.title: Knowing the Father
blocks.body:
Jesus defines eternal life Himself: "this is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent" (John 17:3). Eternal life is a relationship before it is a duration: the life of the Father and the Son shared with us by the Spirit.

That is why John can say believers already *have* eternal life (John 5:24; 1 John 5:12). The life of the age to come has arrived early in Jesus. It begins now, in communion, and is completed in the resurrection.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.body: Augustine argued against those in his day who hoped hell would end that the same word "eternal" governs both punishment and life in Matt 25:46. If one is endless, he reasoned, so must the other be. His argument became the standard Western reading. Augustine's argument from the parallel became the classic response to hopes of universal restoration in the Western church, and it still carries much weight. Critics reply that *aiōnios* qualifies each noun according to its own nature, so the parallel need not mean identical duration.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0166
blocks.body: Origen hoped that God's purpose would end in the restoration of all rational beings to Him, so that the end would be like the beginning, with God "all in all" (1 Cor 15:28). He read the "ages" of Scripture as a long process of correction and return. This view was later condemned and is a minority position. His hope rested more on God's goodness and on texts such as 1 Cor 15:28 than on the meaning of *aiōnios* alone.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0165H
blocks.title: Age and for ever
blocks.body:
*Aiōn* means "age, lifetime, long period". The database splits it into two senses: the "age" sense (G0165G, e.g. "this age", "the age to come") and this sense, mostly in phrases like *eis ton aiōna*, "into the age", i.e. "for ever" (85 times). Doubled forms like *eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn*, "to the ages of the ages" (Gal 1:5; Rev 1:18), are the strongest Greek way of saying "for ever and ever".

The same noun therefore covers both a bounded era ("the present evil age", Gal 1:4) and limitless duration. Context decides.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0165H
blocks.body:
Jews of Jesus' day thought in two ages: "this age", marked by sin and foreign rule, and "the age to come", when God would set things right (Matt 12:32; Eph 1:21). Doxologies such as "blessed be the LORD from everlasting to everlasting" (Ps 106:48) used *olam* in the same way that Greek used *aiōn*.

The disciples' question "what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?" (Matt 24:3) came right after Jesus predicted the temple's destruction. In their minds the temple's fall and the end of the age belonged together.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0165H
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *aiōn* translates Hebrew *olam*, "long time, antiquity, perpetuity" (e.g. "for ever" in Ps 89:1).

The Vulgate used *saeculum*, "age, generation", giving the liturgical phrase *in saecula saeculorum*, "to the ages of ages". English "secular" comes from the same root.

The KJV often rendered *aiōn* as "world", so *synteleia tou aiōnos* became "the end of the world" (Matt 13:39; 24:3; 28:20). Modern versions mostly say "end of the age", which is closer to the Greek and changes how Matt 24 is read.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0165H
blocks.title: The new age has begun
blocks.body:
Jesus brought the age to come into the middle of this age. "The ends of the ages have come" upon the first Christians (1 Cor 10:11), and Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin (Heb 9:26).

A partial-preterist reading takes "the end of the age" in Matt 24:3 as the end of the old covenant order, sealed in the fall of the temple in AD 70, within the generation Jesus named (Matt 24:34). That frees the church from fearing the "end of the world" and points it to the work of the new age: discipling the nations, with the promise "I am with you always, to the end of the age" (Matt 28:20).

The doubled phrase "to the ages of the ages" then celebrates the unending reign of the Father and the Lamb (Rev 5:13).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0165H
blocks.body: Gary DeMar argues that "the end of the age" in Matt 24:3 refers to the end of the Jewish covenant age, which came with the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, not the end of the physical world. He stresses that the KJV's "end of the world" misled later readers. This partial-preterist reading is held by a minority, mainly among Reformed postmillennialists, while most interpreters see at least part of Matt 24 as referring to the final end. It shapes how one reads the urgency of Jesus' warnings to His own generation.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.title: A valley outside Jerusalem
blocks.body:
*Geenna* (12 times) is the Greek form of Hebrew *Ge Hinnom*, "Valley of Hinnom", a ravine on the south and west sides of Jerusalem. Eleven uses are on Jesus' lips (e.g. Matt 5:22, 29-30; 10:28; 23:33; Mark 9:43-47; Luke 12:5); the twelfth is James 3:6, where the tongue is "set on fire by Gehenna".

It is a real place-name used as a symbol of judgement. It is not the same word as *Hadēs*, the realm of the dead.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.body:
The Valley of Hinnom was where kings of Judah burned children in fire at Topheth (2 Kgs 23:10; Jer 7:31). Jeremiah announced that it would be renamed "the Valley of Slaughter", because the dead of Jerusalem would lie unburied there when the city fell (Jer 7:32-33; 19:6-7).

Isaiah ends with corpses of rebels outside the city, "their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched" (Isa 66:24), the image Jesus uses in Mark 9:48. By Jesus' day Jewish writers used Gehenna for the place of the judgement of the wicked (1 Enoch 27; 4 Ezra 7:36).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.body:
*Ge Hinnom* appears in the Septuagint mostly as a place-name (e.g. Josh 18:16). The Greek *geenna* follows Aramaic pronunciation.

The Vulgate kept the word as *gehenna*. The KJV translated it "hell", as it did *hadēs*, *tartaroō* (2 Pet 2:4) and often Hebrew *sheol*. Merging several different words into one English word produced a single, uniform picture of hell that the original vocabulary does not have. Many modern versions print "hell" with a note; some, and many commentaries, keep "Gehenna".

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.title: Was Gehenna a rubbish dump?
blocks.body: A common sermon illustration says Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning rubbish dump. There is no ancient evidence for this; the idea first appears in a medieval Jewish commentary around AD 1200. The valley's significance comes from its history of child sacrifice and Jeremiah's prophecy of slaughter, not from refuse fires. The real background is more striking: Jesus chose a place associated with Israel's worst idolatry and with a prophecy of national catastrophe. Preachers should drop the rubbish-dump illustration and point to Jeremiah instead.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.title: Four readings
blocks.body:
**What did Jesus mean by Gehenna?** Readings differ:

- *Eternal conscious punishment* after death (the majority historic Western view).
- *Final destruction* (conditional immortality): "destroy both soul and body in Gehenna" (Matt 10:28).
- *Purifying judgement* that ends in restoration (a minority strand from some Church Fathers onwards).
- *Historical-prophetic warning:* following Jeremiah, Jesus warned that a nation choosing violence would end as corpses in the valley, fulfilled in AD 70 (Matt 23:33-38).

These are not all mutually exclusive; some combine the historical warning with a final judgement.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.title: A warning given with tears
blocks.body:
Jesus' Gehenna sayings are fierce, and they are spoken mostly to insiders: disciples tempted to despise others (Matt 5:22) and religious leaders who shut people out of the kingdom (Matt 23:13-33). Gehenna is where the way of contempt, violence and self-rule ends.

Read through Jeremiah, Jesus was warning His own generation of the catastrophe their path would bring, and He wept over the city as He did so (Luke 19:41-44). The judge is the same Jesus who forgave from the cross. Whatever Gehenna finally means, it cannot contradict the character of the Father revealed in Him.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1067
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that Jesus' warnings about Gehenna, in their first setting, were largely warnings of the national disaster that would fall on Jerusalem if it refused His way of peace. He does not deny a final judgement, but holds that the original hearers would have heard Jeremiah's valley of slaughter. This reading is a minority one, but it takes seriously the way Jesus repeatedly tied His warnings to 'this generation' (Matt 23:36) and to the fate of the temple and city. It does not on its own decide questions about the final state.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on Jesus' warnings of judgement)

blocks.subject: lemma:G0086
blocks.title: The realm of the dead
blocks.body:
*Hadēs* (10 times) is the Greek name for the underworld, the realm of the dead. In the New Testament it stands for death's domain rather than a place of final punishment: Jesus was not abandoned to Hades (Acts 2:27, 31), He holds "the keys of death and Hades" (Rev 1:18), and at the end "death and Hades" are themselves thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14).

Only Luke 16:23 portrays torment in Hades, in a parable. "The gates of Hades" (Matt 16:18) means the power of death.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0086
blocks.body:
In Greek myth Hades was both a god and his gloomy kingdom beneath the earth, with gates and guards. Jews used the same word for Sheol, the shadowy place where all the dead go (Gen 37:35).

Matthew sets "the gates of Hades" at Caesarea Philippi (Matt 16:13-18), a site with a cave sacred to the god Pan, regarded locally as an entrance to the underworld. Second Temple writings began to divide the realm of the dead into compartments for righteous and wicked (1 Enoch 22), which helps explain Luke 16.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0086
blocks.body:
The Septuagint used *hadēs* for Hebrew *sheol* (e.g. Ps 16:10, quoted in Acts 2:27). This is the bridge that made a Greek mythological word the standard term for the biblical realm of the dead.

The Vulgate rendered it *infernus*, "the lower place", from which comes "descended into hell" (*descendit ad inferos*) in the Apostles' Creed. The KJV used "hell" for *hadēs* (and "grave" once, 1 Cor 15:55). Modern versions usually keep "Hades" to distinguish it from Gehenna.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0086
blocks.title: Christ harrowing Hades
blocks.body:
Hades is not the Father's victory over us but death's hold on us, and Jesus went into it to break it. The early church sang of Christ descending to the dead and preaching even there (1 Pet 3:19; 4:6), and the Eastern icon of the resurrection shows Him trampling the gates of Hades and pulling Adam and Eve out by the wrist.

"The gates of Hades shall not prevail" (Matt 16:18) means the church is not on the defensive: gates do not attack. It is death's stronghold that is under siege. Christ holds its keys (Rev 1:18), and in the end it is emptied and destroyed (Rev 20:13-14).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0086
blocks.body: Michael Heiser connects Jesus' words at Caesarea Philippi with the region's association with rebellious divine beings and the gate of the underworld near Mount Hermon. On his reading, Jesus deliberately chose this place to announce that His church would storm the gates of the realm of death and the powers behind it. This reading has become popular but remains a minority view among scholars. Whether or not every detail holds, the geography of Caesarea Philippi gives the saying a vivid setting.

citations.ref: The Unseen Realm (on Caesarea Philippi and the gates of Hades)

blocks.subject: lemma:G2098
blocks.title: Royal good news
blocks.body:
*Euangelion* (76 times) means "good news, glad announcement" (*eu*, "good" + *angelia*, "message"). In classical Greek it could also mean the reward given to a messenger who brought good news.

In the New Testament it is the announcement of what God has done in Jesus: "the gospel of God concerning His Son ... declared to be Son of God in power by His resurrection" (Rom 1:1-4). Mark opens with "the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1). The gospel is first news about a person and an event, then an invitation.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2098
blocks.body:
In the Roman world *euangelia* announced public events: a victory, an heir's birth, an emperor's accession. A famous inscription from Priene (9 BC) says that the birthday of Augustus, the "saviour" who ended war, was "the beginning of the good news" for the world.

Isaiah's herald brings good news of God's reign: "your God reigns!" (Isa 52:7; 40:9; 61:1). When Christians announced *the* good news that Jesus is Lord and Saviour, they drew on Isaiah and implicitly challenged the imperial gospel.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2098
blocks.body:
The Septuagint uses the verb *euangelizomai* for Hebrew *basar*, "to bring news", especially in Isaiah (Isa 40:9; 52:7; 61:1). Jesus reads Isa 61:1 in Nazareth as fulfilled in Him (Luke 4:18-21).

The Vulgate borrowed the word as *evangelium*, giving "evangelical" and "evangelist". Old English rendered it *godspel*, "good tidings", which became "gospel" in Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2098
blocks.title: News, not advice
blocks.body:
The gospel is not first advice about how to get to heaven, nor a contract to sign. It is news: the Father has, in His Son, defeated death, forgiven the world and opened His family to all (2 Cor 5:19; Col 2:13-15). Jesus preached it before the cross as "the gospel of the kingdom" (Matt 4:23), and the apostles preached it after the resurrection as news of the risen Lord.

Good news is received by believing it, not by earning it. Jesus is the content of the gospel and also its clearest picture: the God the gospel announces looks like Him.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2098
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that for Paul "the gospel" is the royal announcement that the crucified and risen Jesus is Lord, Israel's Messiah and the world's true king. Justification by faith is a consequence of the gospel rather than its content. Wright does not deny that individuals are forgiven and saved through the gospel; he argues that this is the fruit of the announcement rather than its centre. Critics worry this separates the gospel from personal salvation; supporters say it restores the New Testament's own emphasis on Jesus' lordship.

citations.ref: Justification: God's Plan and Paul's Vision (on the gospel)

blocks.subject: lemma:G2962G
blocks.title: Lord: the divine name in Greek
blocks.body:
*Kyrios* means "lord, master, owner", and was also a polite "sir" (John 4:11). This sense (626 times) is *kyrios* used of God or of Jesus as Lord. The database keeps a separate sense for human masters (G2962H).

The early confession "Jesus is Lord" (Rom 10:9; 1 Cor 12:3; Phil 2:11) applied to Jesus the very word Greek-speaking Jews used for the God of Israel. Paul quotes "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Joel 2:32) and means Jesus (Rom 10:13).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2962G
blocks.body:
In the Greco-Roman world *kyrios* was used of slave-owners, patrons, gods, and increasingly of the emperor. Saying "Caesar is Lord" became a test of loyalty. In the account of Polycarp's martyrdom (about AD 155), officials ask him what harm there is in saying "Lord Caesar" and offering incense; he refuses.

For Jews reading Greek, *Kyrios* in Scripture meant the LORD, Israel's God. Confessing Jesus as *Kyrios* placed Him within that identity.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2962G
blocks.body:
Jews did not pronounce God's name YHWH aloud but said *Adonai*, "my Lord". Most Septuagint manuscripts follow this by writing *Kyrios* for YHWH. Some early Greek manuscripts (e.g. Papyrus Fouad 266, first century BC) instead write the Hebrew letters of the name, so whether the very first Greek translators used *Kyrios* is debated.

The Vulgate uses *Dominus*. The KJV prints "LORD" in capitals where Hebrew has YHWH and "Lord" for *Adonai*, and "Lord" for *kyrios* in the New Testament. Phil 2:10-11 applies Isa 45:23, words of YHWH, to Jesus.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2962G
blocks.title: The Lord who serves
blocks.body:
"Jesus is Lord" is the church's first creed. It means the LORD who rescued Israel from Egypt has come in person, and that He looks like Jesus: washing feet, touching lepers, forgiving enemies. His lordship is the lordship of the servant (Mark 10:42-45; Phil 2:6-11).

That gives us confidence about the Father. There is no darker, hidden "Lord" behind Jesus. The Son is the exact imprint of the Father's being (Heb 1:3), so whatever we learn of God's lordship elsewhere in Scripture we read in the light of His face.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1577
blocks.title: The assembly
blocks.body:
*Ekklēsia* (114 times) means "assembly, gathering". It comes from *ek-kaleō*, "to call out", but in ordinary use it simply meant a meeting of people summoned together, not a group "called out" of the world.

In the New Testament it can mean a local gathering ("the church in your house", Phlm 2), all believers in a city (1 Cor 1:2), or the whole people of God (Matt 16:18; Eph 1:22-23). It always refers to people, never to a building.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1577
blocks.body:
In Greek cities the *ekklēsia* was the citizen assembly that met to make decisions. Luke uses it of the riotous town meeting in Ephesus (Acts 19:32, 39, 41).

For Jews, the word recalled Israel gathered before God at Sinai, "the day of the assembly" (Deut 4:10; 9:10). The early Christians chose *ekklēsia* rather than *synagōgē* for themselves, perhaps to claim the identity of Israel assembled before God and to mark themselves as a public body under another Lord. Ignatius (about AD 110) is the first known writer to call it "the catholic church", meaning the whole church gathered around Jesus.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1577
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *ekklēsia* translates Hebrew *qahal*, "assembly, congregation" (Deut 4:10; 1 Kgs 8:14). *Qahal* is also sometimes rendered *synagōgē*.

The Vulgate borrowed it as *ecclesia*. Tyndale translated it "congregation", which Thomas More attacked. The rules given to the KJV translators directed that "the old ecclesiastical words" be kept, naming "church" rather than "congregation". English "church" itself comes from Greek *kyriakon*, "belonging to the Lord", not from *ekklēsia*.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1577
blocks.title: The Father's household
blocks.body:
The church is the family of the Father gathered around the Son by the Spirit. It is "the household of God" (Eph 2:19) and "the body of Christ" (1 Cor 12:27), not an institution the gospel created alongside itself.

Jesus says "I will build my *ekklēsia*" (Matt 16:18): the gathering belongs to Him and its life is His. That is why Paul calls the church "the fullness of Him who fills all in all" (Eph 1:23). In a postmillennial hope, this assembly is the advancing embassy of a kingdom that will fill the earth, a city set on a hill that does not hide.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.title: Trust and faithfulness
blocks.body:
*Pistis* (240 times in this sense) means "trust, confidence", and also "faithfulness, loyalty, reliability", and sometimes "a pledge" or "proof" (Acts 17:31). It is the noun linked to *pisteuō*, "to trust", and *pistos*, "faithful".

In the New Testament it is personal trust in God and in Jesus, the kind that relies on someone and stays loyal to them. It is never mere agreement with ideas: Abraham's faith is trust in a God who gives life to the dead (Rom 4:17-21), and faith "works through love" (Gal 5:6).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.body:
In the Roman world *pistis* (Latin *fides*) was the glue of patronage and friendship: the loyalty a client owed a patron and the reliability a patron showed a client. Rome even honoured *Fides* as a goddess of good faith in agreements.

So when Paul speaks of "the obedience of faith" among the nations (Rom 1:5; 16:26), his hearers would hear trust and allegiance together. Faith is a relationship of reliance and loyalty, not a private opinion.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *pistis* most often renders Hebrew *emunah*, "steadiness, faithfulness" (e.g. Hab 2:4; Ps 33:4). Habakkuk's "the righteous shall live by his faithfulness" appears in the Septuagint as "by *my* faithfulness" (God's), and Paul quotes it without either pronoun (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11).

The Vulgate uses *fides*. The KJV translates *pistis Iēsou Christou* literally: "by the faith of Jesus Christ" (Gal 2:16; Rom 3:22), while most modern versions read "faith in Jesus Christ", often with "faithfulness of Jesus Christ" in a note.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.title: The pistis Christou debate
blocks.body:
**"Faith in Christ" or "the faithfulness of Christ"?** Paul's Greek phrase *pistis Christou* (Gal 2:16, 20; Rom 3:22, 26; Phil 3:9) can be read two ways:

- *Objective genitive:* our faith in Christ (the traditional Protestant reading).
- *Subjective genitive:* Christ's own faith or faithfulness, His trusting obedience to the Father unto death, by which we are set right.

Scholars are divided, and many now argue that both are in view: we are saved by Christ's faithfulness, received by our trust in Him.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.body:
**How faith became an instrument.** In the Reformation debates, faith was defined against works. Justification was treated as a legal verdict, and faith as the instrument that receives Christ's righteousness credited to the believer. This protected grace from human merit, but it could reduce faith to the moment of accepting a legal transfer.

Calvin's own definition was warmer: faith is a firm and certain knowledge of God's benevolence towards us, founded on the promise in Christ and sealed in our hearts by the Spirit. Relational readers build on that: faith is trusting the Father's goodwill as revealed in Jesus.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.title: Sharing the Son's trust
blocks.body:
Faith is not the price we pay for salvation; it is opening our hands to the Father who has already given Himself in His Son. "I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me" (Gal 2:20).

Jesus is the faithful one: He trusted His Father all the way to the cross (Heb 12:2, "the pioneer and perfecter of faith"). Our faith is joining His. We do not manufacture trust to get God on our side; we are drawn by the Spirit into the Son's own confidence in the Father.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4102G
blocks.body: T. F. Torrance argued for the "vicarious humanity" of Christ: Jesus believed, obeyed and worshipped the Father as one of us and on our behalf, so that our faith rests on His faithfulness. Our faith is a sharing in Christ's own faith, not a human work added to His. This view is attractive to relational theology because it removes the anxiety of whether one has 'enough' faith: the decisive believing has been done by Christ in our humanity, and we are invited to share in it. Critics fear it can weaken the call to personal response.

citations.ref: The Mediation of Christ (on the faith of Christ)

blocks.subject: lemma:G4100
blocks.title: To trust oneself to someone
blocks.body:
*Pisteuō* (239 times) means "to trust, rely on, believe", and also "to entrust" something to someone (Luke 16:11; Gal 2:7).

It can mean believing that something is true (John 11:27), believing someone's word (John 4:21), or trusting in a person. John's Gospel favours *pisteuō eis*, "to believe *into*", stressing trust that moves towards and rests in Jesus (John 3:16; 14:1). Strikingly, John never uses the noun *pistis*; for him faith is always a verb, something you do towards a person.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4100
blocks.body:
James notes that bare belief in facts is not enough: "even the demons believe, and shudder" (Jas 2:19). For first-century Jews, believing God meant trusting His promises as Abraham did (Gen 15:6) and Israel did at the sea, when they "believed the LORD and His servant Moses" (Exod 14:31).

In the Greco-Roman world, to *pisteuein* someone was to place confidence in them, much as one entrusted goods or a cause to a reliable friend or patron.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4100
blocks.body:
The Septuagint uses *pisteuō* mainly for the Hebrew causative *he'emin* from the root *aman*, "to be firm" (the root of "Amen"). To believe is to lean one's weight on something solid: "If you will not believe, you will not be established" (Isa 7:9) is a wordplay on that root.

The Vulgate uses *credere*. English "believe" comes from an old Germanic word related to "lief" (dear), originally meaning to hold dear or trust. The KJV uses "believe" throughout; some modern scholars suggest "trust" brings out the personal sense better.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4100
blocks.title: Resting your weight on Him
blocks.body:
To believe is to let your weight rest on Jesus. "Let not your hearts be troubled: believe in God, believe also in me" (John 14:1). It is the stance of a child towards a trustworthy father.

John's "believe into" fits the relational gospel: faith carries us into union with the Son, "that believing you may have life in His name" (John 20:31). We do not believe in order to make God loving; we believe because the love of the Father has been made visible in Jesus (1 John 4:16, "we have come to know and to believe the love God has for us").

blocks.subject: lemma:G5485
blocks.title: Gift, favour and thanks
blocks.body:
*Charis* (155 times) means "favour, goodwill, gift", and also the "thanks" given in return (1 Cor 15:57, "thanks be to God"; compare *eucharistia*, "thanksgiving"). It can also mean "charm, attractiveness" (Luke 4:22, "gracious words").

In the New Testament it is God's generous, unearned goodwill, shown supremely in Jesus: "the Word became flesh ... full of grace and truth ... from His fullness we have all received, grace upon grace" (John 1:14, 16). It is also the power of that goodwill at work in people (1 Cor 15:10).

blocks.subject: lemma:G5485
blocks.body:
*Charis* was a key word of ancient patronage and gift-giving. A benefactor gave a gift; the recipient returned gratitude, honour and loyalty. The Roman philosopher Seneca pictured the three Graces dancing hand in hand to show this circle of giving, receiving and returning.

Gifts were usually given to "worthy" recipients who could reciprocate. Paul's gospel overturns that: God gives to the unworthy, "while we were still sinners" (Rom 5:8). Yet grace still creates a relationship of grateful response, not a transaction with no ties.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5485
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *charis* usually renders Hebrew *chen*, "favour", as in Noah "found favour in the eyes of the LORD" (Gen 6:8). God's covenant love, *chesed*, is usually rendered *eleos*, "mercy", but New Testament *charis* gathers up much of its meaning.

The Vulgate uses *gratia* (compare *gratis*, "free"). Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions use "grace", with "favour" in some places (Luke 2:52) and "thanks" where the sense is gratitude.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5485
blocks.body:
**How grace became a substance and a ledger.** In the medieval West, grace was often described as a quality God infuses into the soul through the sacraments, enabling meritorious works that God then rewards. Grace and merit became a system of accounting.

The Reformers protested by defining grace as God's unmerited favour, a disposition in God rather than a substance in us, and justification as His gracious verdict. Both sides, however, framed grace largely within questions of merit and law.

Relational readers stress that grace is God giving *Himself*: the Father's self-gift in the Son and the Spirit, which makes us His children.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5485
blocks.title: God giving Himself
blocks.body:
Grace is not a thing God hands across a counter; it is the Father sharing Himself. "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Cor 13:14) are one movement of Trinitarian love towards us.

Grace came "through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17), so it looks like Him: eating with sinners, restoring Peter, forgiving executioners. It trains us (Titus 2:11-12), not by threat but by the security of being loved. Thanksgiving, *eucharistia*, is grace returning to its source.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5485
blocks.body: James B. Torrance stressed that God's covenant is a covenant of grace, not a contract. God's love is unconditional in its origin, though it carries unconditional obligations of response. Turning grace into a contract ("if you repent, God will love you") makes forgiveness conditional on us and distorts the gospel. His distinction has been widely used by authors who stress the Father's prior, unconditional love and the call to respond to it in thanksgiving and obedience rather than to earn it.

citations.ref: Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace (on covenant and contract)

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.title: To set right
blocks.body:
*Dikaioō* (39 times) means "to put right, to declare or show to be in the right, to vindicate". In law courts it meant to acquit or rule in someone's favour. It can also mean "to set free" (Rom 6:7, "the one who has died *dedikaiōtai* from sin", i.e. is freed from it) and "to show to be right" (Luke 7:35, "wisdom is justified by all her children").

Paul uses it for God's act of setting people right with Himself through Christ (Rom 3:24-26; 5:1; Gal 2:16). It belongs to the same family as *dikaiosynē*, "righteousness, justice", and *dikaios*, "righteous".

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.body:
In Israel, judges were to "justify the righteous and condemn the wicked" (Deut 25:1); justifying the wicked was an abomination (Prov 17:15). The judge's task was to vindicate those in the right and rescue the oppressed (Ps 82:3).

Against that background, Paul's statement that God "justifies the ungodly" (Rom 4:5) is shocking. God does what no human judge may do, not by pretending the ungodly are good, but by making them right through union with Christ, who was raised for their justification (Rom 4:25).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *dikaioō* mainly renders forms of Hebrew *tsadaq*, "to be in the right", especially the causative "to put in the right, vindicate" (Isa 53:11, "my righteous servant shall make many righteous").

The Vulgate rendered it *iustificare*, literally "to make just". Medieval theology took this as "to make righteous" by an inner change. The Reformers argued it meant "to declare righteous". English "justify" follows the Latin; some scholars prefer "rightwise" or "put right" to keep the link with "righteousness".

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.body:
**How the legal reading arose.** Augustine, reading Latin *iustificare*, took justification to mean God making the ungodly righteous by grace. Medieval theology developed this into a process of infused righteousness.

The Reformers, re-reading the Greek and Hebrew court language, defined justification as a forensic declaration: God pronounces sinners righteous on account of Christ's righteousness credited to them. Calvin called it God's acceptance of us into His favour as righteous. Trent replied that justification includes inner renewal. Later Reformed theology, including Charles Hodge, set it firmly in a courtroom of law and penalty.

Relational authors keep the "declaration" but place it within covenant and union: God's verdict is His welcome of us as His children in Christ, not a bookkeeping transfer.

citations.ref: On the Spirit and the Letter 26.45
Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification, ch. 7

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.title: Put right with the Father
blocks.body:
To be justified is to be put right with the Father: welcomed, vindicated and made a member of His family. "Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God" (Rom 5:1). The fruit of justification is relationship.

The tax collector who prayed "God, be merciful to me" went home justified (Luke 18:13-14), before any sacrifice was offered, simply by throwing himself on God's mercy. Jesus shows the heart of it: the Father sets things right by restoring people, not by merely balancing accounts. In Christ's death and resurrection God put the world right, and faith receives that new standing as gift.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that in Paul justification is God's declaration that a person belongs to the one covenant family promised to Abraham, the family whose single badge is faith in Jesus. It is lawcourt language used within the larger story of God's covenant to put the world right, rather than a description of how individuals are saved from punishment.

citations.ref: Justification: God's Plan and Paul's Vision

blocks.subject: lemma:G1344
blocks.body: Darrin Snyder Belousek argues that biblical justice is primarily restorative: God's righteousness is His saving action to make right what is wrong, not retributive balancing. He reads justification in Paul in that light and challenges the penal framework of satisfaction. His work draws on both Old Testament justice language and on Paul, and it is often cited by those who prefer restorative and Christus Victor frameworks for the atonement. It remains a minority position among evangelical scholars, many of whom defend a penal reading.

citations.ref: Atonement, Justice, and Peace (on God's justice and justification)

blocks.subject: lemma:G0266
blocks.title: Missing the mark and a ruling power
blocks.body:
*Hamartia* (172 times) means "sin, failure, wrongdoing". The related verb *hamartanō* was used in early Greek for missing a target, which is the basis of the popular explanation "missing the mark". In everyday Greek it simply meant error or wrongdoing.

In Paul *hamartia* is often more than individual acts. Sin is pictured as a power: it "entered the world" (Rom 5:12), "reigned in death" (Rom 5:21), enslaves (Rom 6:17) and pays wages (Rom 6:23). John defines sin as lawlessness (1 John 3:4) but also says Jesus "takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0266
blocks.body:
In Greek tragedy, *hamartia* was a fatal error or flaw that brought a hero down (Aristotle, Poetics 13). For Jews, sin was rebellion against God and breach of the covenant (Ps 51:4), dealt with by sacrifice, repentance and the Day of Atonement (Lev 16).

The Septuagint even uses *hamartia* for the "sin offering" itself (e.g. Lev 4:24), which is why some read 2 Cor 5:21, "He made Him to be sin who knew no sin", as "made Him a sin offering". That reading is debated.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0266
blocks.body:
The Septuagint uses *hamartia* chiefly for Hebrew *chatta't*, "sin, sin offering", and also for *avon*, "iniquity", and *pesha'*, "transgression".

The Vulgate uses *peccatum*. One Latin rendering became famous: Rom 5:12 says death spread to all "because (*eph' hō*) all sinned", but the Latin read *in quo omnes peccaverunt*, "in whom all sinned", suggesting all sinned in Adam. The KJV ("for that all have sinned") and modern versions follow the Greek.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0266
blocks.body:
**How sin became mainly guilt and debt.** Augustine, using the Latin of Rom 5:12, taught that all humanity was present in Adam and shares his guilt. Anselm defined sin as failing to render God the honour due to Him, a debt that must be repaid or punished. The Reformers sharpened this into the guilt of breaking God's law, deserving penalty, which Christ bore.

These readings take sin seriously, but they frame it chiefly as legal guilt before a judge. Eastern Fathers and relational authors stress sin as sickness, slavery and broken communion: humanity turned away from the Father and fell into corruption and death, which God heals rather than merely pardons.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0266
blocks.title: A sickness and a slave master
blocks.body:
Sin is first a broken relationship before it is a broken rule. It is turning from the Father who gives life, and so it leads to death (Rom 6:23). It is also a slave master that holds humanity captive (John 8:34).

Jesus treated sinners as people to be freed and healed: "Those who are well have no need of a physician" (Mark 2:17). At the cross He "takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29) and condemns Sin itself in the flesh (Rom 8:3), defeating it as an enemy rather than satisfying an angry Father. The cure for sin is union with the One who conquered it.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0266
blocks.body: Athanasius described sin as a turning from the Word, by whom humans were made, so that humanity began sliding back towards the non-existence from which it came. Death and corruption gained a hold. The Word took a body to reverse this from within, restoring incorruption and life. This is an ontological rather than primarily legal picture of sin: the problem is not only guilt but a fatal drift away from the source of life. It became characteristic of Eastern Orthodox thought and is important for relational readings today.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0859
blocks.title: Release
blocks.body:
*Aphesis* (17 times) means "release, letting go, cancellation". It comes from *aphiēmi*, "to send away, let go". It was used of releasing prisoners, freeing slaves and cancelling debts.

In the New Testament it usually means "forgiveness" of sins (Mark 1:4; Acts 2:38; Eph 1:7): sins are released, let go, cancelled. In Luke 4:18 it means "release" for captives and "liberty" for the oppressed. Forgiveness is a form of liberation.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0859
blocks.body:
Israel's law built release into its calendar. Every seventh year debts were to be cancelled (Deut 15:1-2), and every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, slaves were freed and family land returned (Lev 25:10).

Jesus' first sermon in Luke reads Isa 61:1-2, the prophecy of "the year of the Lord's favour", a Jubilee image, and declares it fulfilled "today" (Luke 4:16-21). His hearers would have heard economic, social and spiritual release all together.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0859
blocks.body:
The Septuagint uses *aphesis* for the Jubilee and the sabbatical "release" (Lev 25:10-13; Deut 15:1-3). That is the bridge: New Testament forgiveness carries the overtones of Jubilee.

The Vulgate uses *remissio*. The KJV has both "remission of sins" (Matt 26:28; Acts 2:38) and "forgiveness of sins" (Eph 1:7), and in Luke 4:18 "deliverance to the captives" and "to set at liberty". Modern versions mostly have "forgiveness", with "release" or "liberty" in Luke 4.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0859
blocks.body:
**How release became remission of penalty.** In Western theology forgiveness was increasingly analysed in legal terms: sin incurred guilt and punishment, and forgiveness meant the judge remitting the penalty because it had been paid. Heb 9:22 ("without shedding of blood there is no *aphesis*") was read as a general law that God cannot forgive until punishment is executed.

Medieval practice distinguished the remission of guilt from remission of temporal punishment, which led to indulgences. Relational readers note that Jesus forgave freely before the cross (Mark 2:5; Luke 7:48), that Heb 9:22 describes the old covenant's purification rites, and that in Christ God releases us from captivity, not merely from a sentence.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0859
blocks.title: Jubilee for the soul
blocks.body:
Forgiveness is Jubilee for the soul. The Father lets go of what we owe and lets us go from what holds us. Jesus spoke forgiveness to the paralysed man before healing him (Mark 2:5) and prayed it over His executioners (Luke 23:34).

In Christ "we have redemption, the *aphesis* of sins" (Eph 1:7). Release is not the end but the doorway to relationship. And because it is release, it is meant to spread: we are to release others as we have been released (Matt 6:12; 18:21-35).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4982
blocks.title: Rescue and healing
blocks.body:
*Sōzō* (106 times) means "to save, rescue, keep safe, heal, make whole". It covers rescue from danger (Matt 8:25, "save us, we are perishing"), healing from disease (Mark 5:34; 10:52), deliverance from demons (Luke 8:36) and rescue from sin and death (Matt 1:21; Rom 10:9).

The related noun *sōtēria* (G4991, 50 times) means "salvation, deliverance, safety". In the Gospels the same word is often used both for healing and for salvation, so the line between body and soul is not sharp.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4982
blocks.body:
In the Roman world gods, generals and emperors were hailed as *sōtēr*, "saviour", for bringing peace, safety and prosperity. Augustus was so honoured in inscriptions. Doctors and healing gods such as Asclepius were also said to "save".

Christians called Jesus "Saviour" (Luke 2:11; Phil 3:20) in a world full of rival saviours. His salvation included the physical: when the bleeding woman touched His cloak, Jesus said "your faith has *sesōken* you", saved and healed (Mark 5:34).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4982
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *sōzō* renders Hebrew *yasha'*, "to deliver, save", the root of the names Joshua and Jesus (*Yeshua*, "the LORD saves"; Matt 1:21). Israel's model of salvation was the Exodus: "the LORD saved Israel that day" (Exod 14:30).

The Vulgate used *salvum facere* and *sanare*; Latin *salus* means both "health" and "salvation". The KJV often translates *sōzō* in healing stories as "made whole" (Mark 5:34; 10:52), which keeps the double sense. Modern versions often split it into "healed" or "saved", which can hide the link.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4982
blocks.title: Made whole
blocks.body:
Salvation is the Father making His children whole. Jesus did not save souls out of bodies; He saved people, healing bodies, restoring minds, forgiving sins and returning outcasts to community. "The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10) is said in Zacchaeus's house, at a meal, after a changed life.

Salvation is rescue from death and from the powers that destroy, and it is healing into union with God. The Father "desires all people to be saved" (1 Tim 2:4), and Jesus, the Saviour of the world (John 4:42), shows what that desire looks like.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4982
blocks.body: Gregory of Nazianzus argued against Apollinarius that Christ must have taken a complete human nature, mind included, because "what has not been assumed has not been healed". Salvation is healing, and the Son heals humanity by taking it into Himself. The principle became a key test of Christology in the early church. It implies that salvation reaches every part of the human person, because the Son has taken every part into union with Himself. It is the theological root of salvation as healing.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3056
blocks.title: Word, message and the Word
blocks.body:
*Logos* (329 times) means "word, saying, message, account, reason". It can be a single saying (Matt 7:24), the gospel message ("the word of God", Acts 4:31), an account to be given (Matt 12:36), or a reason (Acts 10:29).

In John's prologue it is a title: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God ... and the Word became flesh" (John 1:1, 14). Here *Logos* is God's self-expression, His communicating self, now become a human being.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3056
blocks.body:
For Jews, God's word was creative and active: "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made" (Ps 33:6). Wisdom was pictured as God's companion in creation (Prov 8:22-31), and Aramaic paraphrases of Scripture spoke of God's *Memra*, "Word", acting in the world.

Greek philosophers, especially the Stoics, spoke of the *logos* as the rational principle ordering the universe. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria called the Logos God's firstborn and image. John's prologue speaks to both worlds, then says what none of them had imagined: the Logos became flesh.

citations.ref: Philo, On the Confusion of Tongues 146

blocks.subject: lemma:G3056
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *logos* usually renders Hebrew *davar*, "word, matter, thing", as in "the word of the LORD came to" the prophets (e.g. Jer 1:4).

The Vulgate translated John 1:1 *In principio erat Verbum*. Erasmus, in his 1519 edition, used *sermo*, "speech, discourse", and was criticised for it. Tyndale, the KJV and nearly all English versions say "the Word", with a capital to show it is a title for Christ.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3056
blocks.title: Jesus the exegesis of the Father
blocks.body:
If Jesus is the Word, then God is not silent and not hidden behind Him. "No one has ever seen God; the only Son, who is at the Father's side, He has made Him known" (John 1:18). The Greek verb there is *exēgeomai*: Jesus is the exegesis of the Father.

That is what "Jesus is perfect theology" means. Every other word about God, including the words of Scripture, finds its centre and interpretation in the Word made flesh (Heb 1:1-3). The written word points to the living Word (John 5:39-40).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3056
blocks.body: Justin Martyr taught that Christ is the Logos in whom every race of humans has shared, so that those who lived by reason before Christ, such as Socrates, were in a sense Christians. The Logos who became flesh had been at work in all people. Justin's view allowed early Christians to recognise truth wherever it was found while insisting that its fullness is in Christ. It remains an important resource for thinking about the Word's presence in all humanity, though Justin also strongly criticised pagan religion.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3056
blocks.body: Athanasius summed up the purpose of the Incarnation by saying that the Word became human so that we might become divine, sharing by grace in God's life. Clement of Alexandria had earlier said the Word became human so that we might learn from a human how a human may become God. These sayings express the patristic teaching of *theōsis* or deification: not that humans become God by nature, but that by grace they share in the life of the Father through union with the incarnate Son.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2222
blocks.title: Life itself
blocks.body:
*Zōē* (135 times) means "life". Greek had another word, *bios*, used for one's lifespan, livelihood or means of living (Mark 12:44, "all she had to live on"; Luke 15:12, the father "divided his *bios*", his property). *Zōē* is life itself, vitality.

In the New Testament *zōē* is especially the life of God shared with humans: "In Him was life, and the life was the light of men" (John 1:4); "I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly" (John 10:10). Often it is "eternal life", *zōē aiōnios*.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2222
blocks.body:
In the Hebrew Scriptures life is God's gift: the tree of life (Gen 2:9), "I have set before you life and death ... choose life" (Deut 30:19). Life means being in right relation to the God who gives breath.

In the Greco-Roman world, philosophers debated the good life (*bios*), and mystery cults offered union with dying and rising gods. Christians claimed something more concrete: a man had been raised from the dead and now gives His own life to others (John 11:25).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2222
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *zōē* mainly renders Hebrew *chayyim*, "life" (a plural form, suggesting fullness), as in Deut 30:15-19 and Prov 3:18, wisdom is "a tree of life".

The Vulgate uses *vita*. Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions translate it "life". English has no simple way to show the difference between *zōē* and *bios*, which can make "life" in John sound merely biological.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2222
blocks.title: The life of God shared
blocks.body:
*Zōē* is the life the Father has in Himself and has given the Son to have in Himself (John 5:26), poured out on us by the Spirit, "the Spirit of life" (Rom 8:2). Salvation is not just forgiveness of a record but the gift of this life: "whoever has the Son has life" (1 John 5:12).

This life is shared, not owned. It flows from communion: Father, Son and Spirit giving and receiving love. Jesus gives it by laying down His own (John 10:11, 17-18), and it overcomes death from the inside.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2222
blocks.body: Ignatius of Antioch called the Eucharist "the medicine of immortality", the antidote that we should not die but live for ever in Jesus Christ. Life comes by participation in Christ, received in communion. Ignatius wrote these words while being taken to Rome for execution, about AD 110. His language shows how early Christians understood life not as something possessed independently but as received continually through union with the risen Christ. For him the shared bread of the church's gathering was the place where that life was given, and it bound believers to one another as well as to their Lord.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2222
blocks.body: Irenaeus wrote that the glory of God is a living human being, and that human life consists in beholding God. Life is not self-generated; it is received by seeing and sharing in God as He is revealed through the Word. The saying overturns the idea that God's honour competes with human flourishing. A fully alive person, healed and seeing God in Christ, is itself God's glory displayed. It has become one of the most quoted lines in patristic theology.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2842
blocks.title: Sharing a common life
blocks.body:
*Koinōnia* (19 times) means "sharing, partnership, participation, fellowship". It comes from *koinos*, "common, shared". It can mean taking part in something together (Phil 1:5, "partnership in the gospel"; Phil 3:10, "sharing in His sufferings"), a gift shared with others (Rom 15:26, a "contribution" for the poor), or the bond of fellowship itself (Acts 2:42; 1 John 1:3).

Its deepest use is participation in God: "God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son" (1 Cor 1:9); "the *koinōnia* of the Holy Spirit" (2 Cor 13:14).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2842
blocks.body:
*Koinōnia* and *koinōnos* were ordinary business words: James and John were Simon's *koinōnoi*, business partners, in fishing (Luke 5:10). Partners shared capital, risk and profit.

Greek writers also used *koinōnia* for marriage and close friendship, and philosophers prized the proverb "friends have all things in common". The first Jerusalem believers lived that out: "they had all things in common" (Acts 2:44; 4:32).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2842
blocks.body:
*Koinōnia* is rare in the Septuagint; it appears for a partnership or joint deposit (Lev 6:2, 5:21 in Greek numbering) and in the later Wisdom writings (Wis 8:18).

The Vulgate varied: *societas* (1 Cor 1:9), *communicatio* (1 Cor 10:16; 2 Cor 13:14), and *communio*, which gave "communion". The KJV is also varied: "fellowship" (Acts 2:42; 1 John 1:3), "communion" (1 Cor 10:16; 2 Cor 13:14), "contribution" (Rom 15:26), "distribution" (2 Cor 9:13) and "communication" (Phlm 6). The variety hides how often one word is at work.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2842
blocks.title: Sharing the life of the Trinity
blocks.body:
*Koinōnia* is the gospel's goal. "Our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ" (1 John 1:3). We were made to share the life the Father, Son and Spirit share, and by grace we become "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Pet 1:4, *koinōnoi*).

This is not a vague feeling. It is shared bread and cup (1 Cor 10:16), shared money for the poor (Rom 15:26), shared suffering (Phil 3:10). Communion with God always spills over into communion with one another; the Trinity's shared life becomes the church's way of living.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2842
blocks.body: C. Baxter Kruger argues that in Jesus the Father, Son and Spirit have drawn humanity into their shared life. Because the Son became human and took Adam's fallen state into Himself, human beings are already included in His relationship with the Father, and the Spirit's work is to awaken us to that fellowship. This is a minority view, related to the work of T. F. Torrance, and debated by those who stress the need for personal faith.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Undoing of Adam

blocks.subject: lemma:G3306
blocks.title: To stay, remain, dwell
blocks.body:
*Menō* (118 times) means "to stay, remain, abide, dwell, continue". It can be literal, staying in a house (Luke 19:5), or describe something lasting (1 Cor 13:13, "faith, hope and love remain").

John uses it more than any other writer (about 40 times in the Gospel, over 20 in 1 John). For him it describes mutual indwelling: the Father in the Son, the Son in us, us in Him. "Abide in me, and I in you" (John 15:4). The related noun *monē*, "dwelling place", appears in John 14:2, 23.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3306
blocks.body:
In village life, staying with someone meant hospitality and belonging. The first disciples asked Jesus, "where are you staying?" and "they stayed with Him that day" (John 1:38-39). That is where discipleship began: in time spent at home with Him.

The image of the vine (John 15) drew on Israel's old picture of itself as God's vine (Ps 80:8-16; Isa 5:1-7). A branch lives only by remaining joined to the vine.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3306
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *menō* often renders Hebrew verbs for standing firm or enduring, as in "the word of our God will stand (*menei*) for ever" (Isa 40:8, quoted in 1 Pet 1:25).

The Vulgate used *manere*, and in John 14:2 *mansiones multae*, "many dwelling places", from the same verb. The KJV took this over as "In my Father's house are many mansions", which later readers pictured as grand houses in heaven. Modern versions say "rooms" or "dwelling places", which recovers the link with "abide" (John 14:23).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3306
blocks.title: At home in the Father
blocks.body:
*Menō* is the language of union. The Father dwells in the Son (John 14:10); the Son invites us to dwell in Him as He dwells in the Father (John 15:9-10); the Father and the Son come to make their home with us (John 14:23). The "many rooms" of John 14:2 are not first a future real estate promise but a place in the Father's own household, opened by the Son.

Abiding is not anxious effort to stay connected. It is resting in a love that has already taken us in: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love" (John 15:9). "Whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him" (1 John 4:16).

blocks.subject: lemma:G5046
blocks.title: Complete, mature, whole
blocks.body:
*Teleios* (19 times) means "complete, mature, fully developed, having reached its goal". It comes from *telos*, "end, goal". A *teleios* adult is grown up, in contrast to a child (1 Cor 14:20; Heb 5:14).

It does not mainly mean "flawless". "Be *teleioi*, as your heavenly Father is *teleios*" (Matt 5:48) means be whole, complete in love, as your Father is. "Perfect love casts out fear" (1 John 4:18) means love that has come to its full growth.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5046
blocks.body:
In Greek usage *teleios* described a full-grown animal, a sacrifice without defect, or an initiate who had completed a mystery cult's rites. Philosophers spoke of the *teleios* person as one who had reached virtue's goal.

Jewish usage drew on the Hebrew *tamim*, "whole, blameless": Noah was "blameless in his generation" (Gen 6:9), and Israel was to be "blameless before the LORD" (Deut 18:13). That meant wholehearted loyalty, not sinless perfection.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5046
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *teleios* renders Hebrew *tamim* (Gen 6:9; Deut 18:13) and *shalem*, "whole, at peace" (1 Kgs 8:61, "let your heart be wholly true"). Jesus' words in Matt 5:48 echo Deut 18:13 and Lev 19:2.

The Vulgate uses *perfectus*, "finished, complete", and the KJV "perfect". In modern English "perfect" usually means "without any fault", so newer versions often say "mature" (Heb 5:14; Eph 4:13) or "complete" (Jas 1:4), though most keep "perfect" in Matt 5:48.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5046
blocks.title: The Father's perfection is mercy
blocks.body:
Read Matt 5:48 in context. Jesus has just said: love your enemies, because your Father "makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good" (Matt 5:44-45). The Father's perfection is His indiscriminate love. Luke's version says it plainly: "Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36).

So *teleios* is not a demand for flawless performance that drives us to anxiety. It is an invitation to grow up into the family likeness, loving as the Father loves, as children who resemble Him. Christ is the mature human, and we grow "to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ" (Eph 4:13).

blocks.subject: lemma:G5046
blocks.body: Irenaeus taught that humanity was created like a child, not yet mature, and was meant to grow towards perfection over time. God could have given perfection from the start, but humans were not yet able to receive it. Salvation history is God patiently raising His children to maturity in Christ. This picture of growth, rather than a fall from finished perfection, has shaped Eastern theology and relational readings. It sees God as a patient parent and history as education towards maturity, culminating in Christ, the perfect human.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1515
blocks.title: Peace as wholeness
blocks.body:
*Eirēnē* (91 times) means "peace". In classical Greek it mostly meant the absence of war. In the New Testament, shaped by Hebrew *shalom*, it means wholeness, well-being and restored relationships: peace with God (Rom 5:1), peace between enemies (Eph 2:14-17), and inner peace (Phil 4:7).

It is a standard greeting in letters ("grace to you and peace", Rom 1:7) and the risen Jesus' first word to His frightened disciples: "Peace be with you" (John 20:19, 21).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1515
blocks.body:
The Roman Empire celebrated the *Pax Romana*, the peace Augustus brought after civil war. The Senate dedicated the Altar of Peace (*Ara Pacis*) in Rome to it in 9 BC. Roman peace was secured by legions and crucifixion.

Against this, angels announce "on earth peace" at the birth of a different Saviour (Luke 2:14), and Jesus says "my peace I give to you; not as the world gives" (John 14:27). Many scholars think "peace and security" in 1 Thess 5:3 echoes Roman propaganda slogans, though this is debated.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1515
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *eirēnē* translates Hebrew *shalom* in most of its more than 200 occurrences. That transfer gave the Greek word its fuller sense of welfare, health, prosperity and right relationship ("Is it *shalom* with the young man?", 2 Sam 18:29).

The Vulgate uses *pax*. Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions translate "peace". English "peace" tends to sound inward or merely quiet, so readers may miss its social and covenantal depth.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1515
blocks.title: He is our peace
blocks.body:
"He Himself is our peace" (Eph 2:14). In Jesus the Father reconciled the world to Himself, "making peace by the blood of His cross" (Col 1:20). The cross is not the Father's violence finding an outlet but the Son absorbing human violence and answering it with forgiveness.

Christ's peace is therefore not a ceasefire with an offended God, but the restoration of shalom: humans with God, with one another, and with creation. Peacemakers are called "sons of God" (Matt 5:9) because they share the Father's family likeness. In a postmillennial hope, this peace spreads as Isaiah foresaw, until swords become ploughshares (Isa 2:4).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1515
blocks.body: Darrin Snyder Belousek argues that the cross should be understood within God's peacemaking justice: God makes peace by restoring right relationships, overcoming enmity through Christ's self-giving, rather than by inflicting retributive punishment. Atonement and peace belong together. On this view, Paul's language of peace with God (Rom 5:1) and peace between Jew and Gentile (Eph 2:14-17) are two sides of one restoring work. The church's calling to make peace flows directly from the way God has made peace with us in Christ.

citations.ref: Atonement, Justice, and Peace (on peacemaking justice)

blocks.subject: lemma:G4697
blocks.title: Gut-wrenching compassion
blocks.body:
*Splanchnizomai* (about a dozen times) means "to be moved with compassion", literally to feel it in the *splanchna*, the inner organs or "guts", which ancient people treated as the seat of deep emotion.

In the Gospels it is used only of Jesus (e.g. Matt 9:36; 14:14; Mark 1:41; Luke 7:13) and of three figures in His parables: the master who forgives the huge debt (Matt 18:27), the Samaritan (Luke 10:33) and the father of the lost son (Luke 15:20). It names a compassion that leads straight into action.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4697
blocks.body:
In Greek, *splanchna* were originally the innards of a sacrificial animal, eaten at the sacrifice; the active verb *splanchnizō* meant to eat them (2 Macc 6:8). Over time *splanchna* came to mean the feelings, much as English speaks of the heart.

Hebrew had a parallel: *rachamim*, "compassion", from *rechem*, "womb". Deep mercy was felt in the body. When the Samaritan, a despised outsider, is the one "moved with compassion", Jesus deliberately reverses expectations of who shows God's heart (Luke 10:33).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4697
blocks.body:
The verb is almost absent from the Septuagint; the noun *splanchna* appears in later Jewish Greek writings for compassion (e.g. Prov 12:10). The Gospel writers seem to have favoured it as a word for Jesus' own heart.

The Vulgate usually has *misericordia motus*, "moved by mercy". The KJV says "moved with compassion" and, for the noun, "bowels of mercies" (Col 3:12). Modern versions say "had compassion" or "felt compassion". In Mark 1:41 some manuscripts read "moved with anger" instead; scholars debate which is original.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4697
blocks.title: The Father's insides
blocks.body:
This is the word the Gospels use to show us God's insides. When the father sees his ruined son "while he was still a long way off", he is *splanchnistheis*, and he runs, embraces and kisses him before any confession (Luke 15:20). Jesus tells the story to show what the Father is like.

Because Jesus is perfect theology, His gut-level compassion for crowds, lepers and widows (Mark 1:41; Luke 7:13) is not a softer side of a stern God; it is the Father's heart in flesh. This is the inner reality behind every other word for mercy in Scripture.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4697
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argued from Middle Eastern village culture that a dignified patriarch would never run in public. The father in Luke 15 humiliates himself by running, taking the son's shame on himself and reaching him before the village could reject him. Bailey saw this as a picture of the incarnation and the cross. Some scholars question how far modern village customs can be read back into the first century, but Bailey's reading has been widely influential in preaching on Luke 15.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0629
blocks.title: Release from captivity
blocks.body:
*Apolytrōsis* (10 times) means "release, liberation, redemption". It is built on *lytron*, "ransom", and originally meant release by payment of a ransom, but in the New Testament the emphasis is on the release itself.

It describes present freedom: "in Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of trespasses" (Eph 1:7; Col 1:14; Rom 3:24). It also describes the future release of the whole person: "the redemption of our bodies" (Rom 8:23) and "your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:28). In Heb 11:35 it means release from torture.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0629
blocks.body:
In the Greco-Roman world prisoners of war were ransomed and slaves could buy their freedom. Some inscriptions record slaves "sold" to a god so that they might be free, and some scholars think this background shaped Paul's language, though that is debated.

The deeper background is the Exodus. God told Israel "I will redeem you with an outstretched arm" (Exod 6:6) and later reminded them "the LORD redeemed you from the house of slavery" (Deut 7:8). No payment to Pharaoh was involved: redemption meant God's powerful rescue of His people.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0629
blocks.body:
The noun barely appears in the Septuagint, but the verb *lytroō*, "to redeem", is common for God's rescue of Israel from Egypt and exile (Exod 6:6; Isa 43:1; 44:22-24). It renders Hebrew *ga'al* (to act as kinsman-redeemer) and *padah* (to ransom).

The Vulgate uses *redemptio*, "buying back". The KJV and modern versions say "redemption", with "deliverance" in Heb 11:35. The English word suggests a commercial exchange more strongly than the Greek usually does.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0629
blocks.title: Exodus fulfilled
blocks.body:
Redemption is the Exodus fulfilled in Jesus. Humanity was enslaved to sin, death and the powers (Heb 2:14-15); in Christ the Father has come in person to set His children free. The "price" language speaks of what freedom cost: the Son's self-giving even to death, "His blood" (Eph 1:7).

But Scripture never tells us the Father needed paying. The Father is the redeemer, not the one being bought off (Isa 43:1-3). Redemption is not yet complete: we "groan inwardly as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our bodies" (Rom 8:23), when creation itself will be set free.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0629
blocks.body: Irenaeus wrote that the Lord redeemed us by His own blood, giving His soul for our souls and His flesh for our flesh. He insisted that the Word redeemed humanity from the apostasy not by violence but by persuasion, as befitted God, who does not seize what is His by force.
