Irenaeus' contrast between violence and persuasion is important for relational readings: God does not overpower even His enemies by force, but wins humanity back through the self-giving of the Son.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3083
blocks.title: The price of freedom
blocks.body:
*Lytron* means "ransom, price of release". It occurs twice, in the same saying: "the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45; Matt 20:28). Paul has a compound, *antilytron*: Christ "gave Himself as a ransom for all" (1 Tim 2:6).

The word answers the question "what did it cost to set us free?" Jesus' answer: His own life, freely given.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3083
blocks.body:
In the ancient world a *lytron* was paid to free prisoners of war, slaves or condemned persons. Israel's law knew ransoms too: a payment to spare a life (Exod 21:30), the half-shekel "ransom for his life" at the census (Exod 30:12), and the redemption price of the firstborn (Num 3:46-51).

Jesus speaks of ransom in the context of rulers who "lord it over" others (Mark 10:42). His ransom saying redefines greatness as service, with Isaiah's suffering servant in the background (Isa 53:10-12).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3083
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *lytron* renders Hebrew *kopher*, "ransom, covering price" (Exod 21:30; 30:12), *ge'ullah*, "redemption" of land (Lev 25:24-26), and *pidyon*, "redemption money" (Exod 21:30; Num 3:49).

The Vulgate rendered Mark 10:45 *redemptionem pro multis*, "a redemption for many". Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions say "ransom". The Septuagint background shows that *lytron* belonged to family and covenant life in Israel, not only to the slave market. A *lytron* rescued a life or restored what had been lost.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3083
blocks.body:
**How the ransom was interpreted.** The early church asked: ransom paid to whom? Some Fathers, such as Gregory of Nyssa, said it was paid to the devil, who held humanity captive, and pictured Christ's humanity as bait on the hook of His divinity. Gregory of Nazianzus rejected the idea of a payment to either the devil or the Father as a literal transaction.

Anselm rejected any rights of the devil and recast the problem: the debt was owed to God's honour, and Christ paid it as satisfaction. The Reformers moved further to penal substitution, where the "price" is punishment owed to divine justice.

Relational readers return to the earlier picture: the ransom is Christ's self-giving that breaks the captors' hold, paid to no one as a bribe.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3083
blocks.title: Costly liberation
blocks.body:
A ransom is a metaphor for costly liberation. Jesus does not say who receives the payment, and pressing that detail misses His point. The point is that the Son gave Himself, all the way, to set captives free.

The ransom saying belongs with Christus Victor: the strong man is bound and his goods plundered (Mark 3:27); death could not hold the Son (Acts 2:24). The Father is not the kidnapper demanding payment; He is the one who "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all" (Rom 8:32). Love paid the cost of entering our captivity and breaking it open.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3083
blocks.body: Gustaf Aulén argued that the "classic" view of the early church saw the atonement as a divine drama: God in Christ fights and triumphs over the powers that hold humanity in bondage, sin, death and the devil. Ransom language belongs to this victory picture rather than to a legal payment to God. Aulén contrasted this classic view with the later Latin (satisfaction) theory and the subjective (moral influence) theory. His book revived interest in Christus Victor across many traditions, though historians debate how neatly the three types fit the sources.

citations.ref: Christus Victor (on the classic idea of atonement)

blocks.subject: lemma:G3528
blocks.title: To conquer
blocks.body:
*Nikaō* (28 times) means "to conquer, overcome, prevail, win". The noun *nikē* means "victory".

Jesus says, "Take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Revelation uses the word repeatedly: promises "to the one who conquers" (Rev 2:7 and onwards); "the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered" (Rev 5:5); "the Lamb will conquer them" (Rev 17:14). Paul says "do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Rom 12:21).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3528
blocks.body:
*Nikē* was the Greek goddess of victory, Victoria to the Romans. Roman emperors advertised their victories on coins and monuments, and a general's triumph paraded captives through Rome. Christians in Asia Minor, where Revelation was first read, lived amid this imagery.

Revelation's conquerors win not by killing but by dying faithfully: "they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death" (Rev 12:11).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3528
blocks.body:
The verb is uncommon in the Septuagint. Paul quotes one use: "that you may be justified in your words and prevail (*nikēseis*) when you are judged" (Rom 3:4, from Ps 51:4 in Greek).

The Vulgate uses *vincere*, "to conquer". The KJV says "overcome" (John 16:33; Rev 2-3) and "prevail" (Rev 5:5). Modern versions alternate between "conquer" and "overcome"; "conquer" brings out the military irony of Revelation more clearly.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3528
blocks.title: The Lamb who conquers
blocks.body:
Revelation's great surprise is in chapter 5. John is told to look at the conquering Lion and turns to see "a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain" (Rev 5:5-6). God's victory looks like the cross. The powers are defeated not by superior violence but by self-giving love that death cannot hold (Col 2:15).

This is Christus Victor. And because the Lamb has already conquered, the church's calling is hopeful: to overcome evil with good (Rom 12:21) and to see "the kingdom of the world become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ" (Rev 11:15). The victory is won; it is now being worked out in history.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3528
blocks.body: B. B. Warfield read Rev 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse, not as a picture of the second coming but of the victory of Christ through the gospel during the present age. The sword comes from His mouth: the Word conquers the nations, a reading that fits postmillennial hope. Warfield was a leading Princeton theologian and a postmillennialist. His reading of Revelation as a picture of the gospel's victory in history is shared by many in that tradition, though most commentators read Rev 19 as the final return of Christ.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0509
blocks.title: From above, and again
blocks.body:
*Anōthen* (13 times) means "from above", "from the top", "from the beginning", or "again, anew". The temple curtain was torn "from top (*anōthen*) to bottom" (Matt 27:51); Luke investigated "from the beginning" (Luke 1:3); every good gift is "from above" (Jas 1:17).

In John 3:3, 7 Jesus says one must be born *anōthen*. The word can mean both "again" and "from above", and John seems to intend both. Later in the chapter it clearly means "from above" (John 3:31).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0509
blocks.body:
Nicodemus was "a ruler of the Jews" and a teacher of Israel (John 3:1, 10). He hears *anōthen* as "again" and asks how a grown man can re-enter his mother's womb (John 3:4). Misunderstanding is a deliberate technique in John: Jesus speaks of heavenly realities, His hearers take Him literally, and the reader learns the deeper meaning.

Jews of the time spoke of converts as being like newborn children, which may also lie behind the conversation.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0509
blocks.body:
There is no direct Septuagint bridge for the phrase "born *anōthen*".

The Vulgate chose *renatus fuerit denuo*, "born anew". Tyndale and the KJV followed with "born again", and the KJV margin offered "from above". This rendering shaped later revivalist language of being "born again". Many modern versions (e.g. NRSV) read "born from above", with "born again" or "anew" in the margin.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0509
blocks.title: Born of the Father
blocks.body:
To be born from above is to be born of the Father, not to improve yourself. "To all who received Him ... He gave the right to become children of God, who were born not of blood ... but of God" (John 1:12-13). New birth is entrance into the Son's relationship with the Father by the Spirit, who blows where He wills (John 3:8).

It is not a technique, a decision we manufacture, or a badge of a spiritual elite. It is grace from above, as gratuitous as natural birth. And it is cosmic in scope: the same chapter tells us why the Father sent the Son: because He so loved the world (John 3:16).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0509
blocks.body: Justin Martyr, describing Christian baptism to the emperor, quoted Jesus' saying that unless you are born again you cannot enter the kingdom, and connected new birth with baptism, which Christians called "illumination". This is one of the earliest uses of John 3 outside the New Testament. Justin's account, written in the mid-second century, shows that the new-birth language of John 3 was already a central part of how Christians spoke about becoming members of God's family.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1391
blocks.title: Glory
blocks.body:
*Doxa* (166 times) in classical Greek meant "opinion, reputation" (hence "orthodoxy", right opinion). In the New Testament it means "glory": splendour, radiance, honour and the visible presence of God.

"We beheld His glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). God's glory shines "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), and the Son is "the radiance of His glory" (Heb 1:3). Humans "fall short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23) but are destined to share it (Rom 8:18, 21).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1391
blocks.body:
In Greco-Roman culture *doxa* was public reputation and honour, a central value in an honour-and-shame society. People competed for glory through status, office and benefaction.

Jesus confronted this: "How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?" (John 5:44). In John's Gospel His "hour" of glory is the cross (John 12:23-24; 13:31), a place of public shame.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1391
blocks.body:
The meaning of *doxa* changed through the Septuagint, which used it to translate Hebrew *kavod*, "weight, honour, glory", especially for the shining presence of God that filled the tabernacle and temple (Exod 40:34; 1 Kgs 8:11). This shift from "opinion" to "radiant presence" is one of the clearest examples of the Septuagint reshaping a Greek word.

The Vulgate uses *gloria*, and Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions "glory".

blocks.subject: lemma:G1391
blocks.title: Glory with a human face
blocks.body:
Moses asked to see God's glory, and God answered by proclaiming His goodness and His name: merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love (Exod 33:18-19; 34:6). In Jesus that glory is finally seen with a human face (John 1:14).

And the glory is shared. "The glory that You have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one" (John 17:22). The Father's glory is not self-display at our expense but self-giving love, most visible at the cross. We are being transformed "from glory to glory" into the image of the Son (2 Cor 3:18).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1391
blocks.body: Irenaeus wrote that the glory of God is a living human being, and the life of humanity is the vision of God. God's glory is not diminished by our flourishing; it is displayed in it, through the Word who makes the Father visible. The saying unites God's honour with human flourishing: the Father is glorified when His children come fully alive. It has become a touchstone for relational theology.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0025
blocks.title: To love
blocks.body:
*Agapaō* (143 times) means "to love, to value, to be devoted to". The noun is *agapē*. It is the most common verb for love in the New Testament: God's love for the world (John 3:16), the Father's love for the Son (John 3:35; 17:24), and the love commanded of disciples, including love for enemies (Matt 5:44).

It is not always a "higher" love. People can *agapaō* darkness (John 3:19), the praise of others (John 12:43) or "this present age" (2 Tim 4:10). What makes love divine is not the word but its object and source: "God is love" (1 John 4:8, 16).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0025
blocks.body:
Classical Greek had several love words: *erōs* (desire), *philia* (friendship, affection), *storgē* (family affection) and *agapaō* (to be fond of, to welcome). The noun *agapē* was rare before the Septuagint and early Christian writers made it common.

Christians used *agapē* for the shared fellowship meal (Jude 12), and Greek-speaking believers came to see it as a word for a new kind of love: self-giving, extended to strangers and enemies, modelled on the cross (Rom 5:8; 1 John 3:16).

blocks.subject: lemma:G0025
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *agapaō* translates Hebrew *ahav*, "to love", across its whole range: Abraham's love for Isaac (Gen 22:2), love for God and neighbour (Deut 6:5; Lev 19:18), and even Amnon's obsession with Tamar (2 Sam 13:1, 15).

The Vulgate used *diligere* and *amare*, and *caritas* for the noun in 1 Cor 13. That is why the KJV says "charity" there. Tyndale had used "love", which Thomas More criticised. Modern versions say "love" throughout.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0025
blocks.title: Agape versus phileo?
blocks.body: Sermons often say *agapē* is God's unconditional love and *phileō* is mere human affection, and read John 21:15-17 as Peter failing to rise to Jesus' *agapē*. Many scholars doubt this: John uses both verbs for the Father's love for the Son (John 3:35; 5:20) and the Septuagint uses *agapaō* even for sinful love. Others still see a deliberate shift in John 21. The distinction cannot carry the weight often placed on it.

blocks.subject: lemma:G0025
blocks.title: The Trinity's own life
blocks.body:
Love is the Trinity's own life opened to us. Before the world began, the Father loved the Son (John 17:24); the Son loves us "as the Father has loved me" (John 15:9); and the Spirit pours God's love into our hearts (Rom 5:5).

The cross is not a price love had to pay to an angry justice; it is love itself, "God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8). Love is not God's mood at times but His very being. Jesus is how we know what *agapē* means: "By this we know love, that He laid down His life for us" (1 John 3:16).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2434
blocks.title: Atonement for the whole world
blocks.body:
*Hilasmos* occurs twice, both in 1 John: Jesus Christ "is the *hilasmos* for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2), and "In this is love, not that we have loved God but that He loved us and sent His Son to be the *hilasmos* for our sins" (1 John 4:10).

The word family includes *hilaskomai*, "to be merciful, to make atonement" (Luke 18:13; Heb 2:17), and *hilastērion*, the "mercy seat" (Heb 9:5; Rom 3:25). Its meaning, whether appeasing anger (propitiation) or removing sin (expiation), is debated.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2434
blocks.body:
In pagan Greek, the *hilask-* words often meant placating an angry god or person with gifts or sacrifices. In Israel's worship the background was the Day of Atonement, when blood was sprinkled on the mercy seat to cleanse the sanctuary and the people (Lev 16:14-16, 30).

In Israel, God Himself provided the means of atonement: "I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls" (Lev 17:11). Atonement was God's gift to restore relationship, not a human bribe to change His mind.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2434
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint the *hilask-* words render Hebrew *kipper*, "to make atonement, cleanse, cover", and related nouns: "the day of atonement" (Lev 25:9), "the ram of atonement" (Num 5:8). In Ps 130:4 (129:4 in Greek) *hilasmos* renders *selichah*, "forgiveness": "with You there is forgiveness".

The Vulgate rendered *propitiatio*, and the KJV "propitiation". Twentieth-century versions split: the RSV chose "expiation", the NIV and NRSV "atoning sacrifice", the ESV kept "propitiation". The choice reflects a theological debate about whether God's wrath needed appeasing.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2434
blocks.body:
**How propitiation became appeasing justice.** In the satisfaction and penal traditions, *hilasmos* was read as Christ satisfying God's justice by bearing the punishment due to sinners, so turning away God's wrath. Charles Hodge and later Reformed theologians made propitiation, understood as the satisfaction of retributive justice, central to the atonement.

A twentieth-century debate asked whether biblical usage really means placating God or rather wiping away sin. Relational readers note that in 1 John the Father is the subject who sends the Son out of love (1 John 4:10). Whatever *hilasmos* means, God is not the one being changed; sin is what is removed and the relationship is what is restored.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2434
blocks.title: Love sends the remedy
blocks.body:
Read the verse whole: "He loved us and sent His Son to be the *hilasmos*" (1 John 4:10). Love comes first and is the source; the atonement flows from the Father's heart, it does not create it. Jesus is not a third party persuading an unwilling God.

Jesus is the mercy seat: the place where God and humanity meet and sin is cleansed away. And the scope is the whole world (1 John 2:2). In Him God covers, cleanses and heals, absorbing the cost of our sin in His own self-giving and so ending our estrangement.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2434
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that *hilastērion* in Rom 3:25 refers to the mercy seat, the place where God dealt with sin and met His people, and he rejects reading the cross as a "pagan" story of an angry deity being placated by a human victim. In his view, the cross deals with sin within the story of God's covenant and new Passover.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2643
blocks.title: From enemies to friends
blocks.body:
*Katallagē* (4 times) means "reconciliation", the restoring of friendship between estranged parties. The verb *katallassō* means "to reconcile, to change from enmity to friendship" (Rom 5:10; 2 Cor 5:18-20; and of a wife and husband, 1 Cor 7:11).

A striking feature: in Paul, God is always the reconciler and humans (or the world) are the ones reconciled. "God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them" (2 Cor 5:19). Paul never says God had to be reconciled to us.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2643
blocks.body:
*Katallagē* belonged to diplomacy and family life: making peace between warring cities or estranged spouses. Usually the offending party sought to appease the offended.

In 2 Maccabees the Jewish writer prays that God will "be reconciled" to His people after their sins (2 Macc 1:5; 7:33). Paul reverses this direction: the offended party, God, takes the initiative and reconciles His enemies to Himself, at His own cost (Rom 5:10).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2643
blocks.body:
There is no Hebrew equivalent; the word appears in the Greek Old Testament only in the later books like 2 Maccabees.

The Vulgate uses *reconciliatio*. In Rom 5:11 the KJV reads "by whom we have now received the atonement", using the English word "atonement" (at-one-ment, being made one) that Tyndale's translations had popularised. Elsewhere the KJV says "reconciliation" (2 Cor 5:18-19). Over time "atonement" came to mean sacrifice for sin rather than "making at one".

blocks.subject: lemma:G2643
blocks.body:
**How reconciliation became two-sided.** Later Western theology often read reconciliation as mutual: humans were hostile to God, and God's justice was hostile to humans until satisfied. Calvin admitted the paradox, saying God in a wondrous way loved us even while He was angry with us, and that Christ's sacrifice removed the enmity on God's side.

Relational readers note that the Pauline texts consistently make God the subject who reconciles and the world the object. The enmity to be overcome is ours; the Father's love was never withdrawn.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2643
blocks.title: God makes the first move
blocks.body:
Reconciliation is the gospel in one word. The Father did not wait for us to make the first move: "while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son" (Rom 5:10). In Christ He was "not counting their trespasses against them" (2 Cor 5:19).

That is why the message is an appeal, not a threat: "Be reconciled to God" (2 Cor 5:20). Reconciliation is already accomplished from God's side for the world; the invitation is to come home and live in it. It also sends us out: those reconciled are given "the ministry of reconciliation" between people.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2643
blocks.body: T. F. Torrance taught that reconciliation was worked out within the very person of Christ: in uniting divine and human natures in Himself, the Son healed the enmity of human nature from inside and offered a reconciled humanity to the Father. Atonement is not external to the incarnation but takes place in it. On this view, reconciliation is not a transaction outside Jesus that we must try to access, but a reality already accomplished in His humanity, into which the Spirit draws us.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5207
blocks.title: Son
blocks.body:
*Huios* (374 times) means "son". It is used of physical sons, of descendants ("son of David", Matt 1:1), and of anyone sharing a character: "sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17), "a son of peace" (Luke 10:6), "sons of light" (1 Thess 5:5).

Jesus is "the Son" in a unique sense (Mark 1:11; John 1:18), and also "the Son of Man" (Dan 7:13; Mark 14:62). Believers become "sons of God" through faith and the Spirit (Gal 3:26; 4:6), a status Paul calls *huiothesia*, "adoption as sons" (Rom 8:15; Eph 1:5).

blocks.subject: lemma:G5207
blocks.body:
In the ancient world, a son was the heir, carrying the family name, honour and inheritance. Roman adoption was a legal act, often of adults, that gave the adopted person a new family, a new name and full rights of inheritance. Augustus himself was adopted in Julius Caesar's will.

When Paul speaks of *huiothesia*, he uses a Roman legal idea to say that believers, Jew and Gentile, male and female (Gal 3:28), have the full status of heirs, "heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ" (Rom 8:17).

blocks.subject: lemma:G5207
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *huios* renders Hebrew *ben*, "son", including Israel as God's son (Exod 4:22; Hos 11:1) and the king as God's son (2 Sam 7:14; Ps 2:7).

The Vulgate uses *filius*, and *adoptio filiorum* for adoption. The KJV usually says "son" but sometimes "children" (Gal 3:26). Some modern versions use "children" more widely for inclusiveness; that is right in substance, since daughters are included (2 Cor 6:18), but it can hide the point that every believer has the heir's status of a son.

blocks.subject: lemma:G5207
blocks.title: Sharing the Son's place
blocks.body:
Sonship is the goal of the gospel. "God sent forth His Son ... to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father!" (Gal 4:4-6). The eternal Son became a son of Adam so that sons and daughters of Adam might share His sonship.

This is not a legal technicality but participation in the Son's own relationship with the Father. We are not slaves trying to earn a place but children already loved, heirs of the whole renewed creation (Rom 8:17-21).

blocks.subject: lemma:G5207
blocks.body: Irenaeus taught that the Word of God became human, and the Son of God became Son of Man, so that humanity, being taken into the Word and receiving adoption, might become sons of God. Union with the incarnate Son is the way into sonship. This "exchange" formula, that He became what we are so that we might become what He is, became central to the theology of the early church. It frames salvation as sonship through participation in the Son, rather than chiefly as a legal acquittal.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3962
blocks.title: Father
blocks.body:
*Patēr* (413 times) means "father". It is used of human fathers, ancestors ("our father Abraham", John 8:39), and above all of God.

The Hebrew Scriptures call God "Father" relatively rarely, about fifteen times (e.g. Deut 32:6; Ps 103:13; Isa 63:16; 64:8; Mal 1:6). In the Gospels it is everywhere: Jesus speaks of "my Father" and "your Father", and in John alone the Father is named more than a hundred times. The name "Father" is the centre of Jesus' teaching about God.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3962
blocks.body:
In Roman society the *paterfamilias* held legal authority (*patria potestas*) over his household, including adult children. In Jewish families the father was head of household, teacher of Torah (Deut 6:7) and giver of blessing.

Jesus' picture of fatherhood reshaped these expectations: a father who runs to a returning son (Luke 15:20), who gives good gifts (Matt 7:11), who sees in secret (Matt 6:6) and who knows our needs before we ask (Matt 6:8).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3962
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *patēr* renders Hebrew *av*, "father". When God is called Father it is often in covenant contexts: Israel as His firstborn (Exod 4:22; Jer 31:9) and the king as His son (2 Sam 7:14).

The Vulgate uses *pater* (*Pater noster*, "Our Father", Matt 6:9). Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions say "Father". Some recent discussion has questioned the name as patriarchal; Christian tradition holds it is a name revealed by the Son, not a projection of human fathers onto God.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3962
blocks.title: Seen in the Son
blocks.body:
"Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Jesus is the full revelation of what the Father is like. There is no hidden God behind Jesus with a different temperament. Wherever the Old Testament's picture of God seems harsh or unclear, we read it through the face of the Son.

God is Father before He is Creator or Judge: eternally the Father of the Son, in the fellowship of the Spirit. Creation and redemption flow from that love. The gospel is the Father sharing His own fatherhood with us in His Son, so that we too say "Our Father" (Matt 6:9).

blocks.subject: lemma:G3962
blocks.body: Athanasius argued that it is more devout and accurate to name God from the Son and call Him Father than to name Him from His works and call Him "Unoriginate". God's first name, revealed by Christ, is Father, which defines who He is in relation to the Son. Against those who called the Son a creature, Athanasius insisted that Father and Son belong together eternally. If God is eternally Father, then love and relationship are not added to God later; they are who God is.

blocks.subject: lemma:G3962
blocks.body: James B. Torrance contrasted a "legal" understanding of God, where God is mainly a lawgiver and judge to be satisfied, with a "filial" one, where God is first the Father who created us for sonship and communion in the Son by the Spirit. He saw the filial purpose as primary. This filial emphasis underlies much relational theology today, which reads law and judgement within the larger purpose of sonship.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4151G
blocks.title: Spirit, breath and wind
blocks.body:
*Pneuma* means "wind, breath, spirit". This sense (372 times) is "spirit": the Holy Spirit, the human spirit (1 Cor 2:11), and other spirits, including "unclean spirits" (Mark 1:23). A separate sense (G4151H) covers "breath" and "wind".

Jesus plays on the double meaning: "The wind (*pneuma*) blows where it wills ... so it is with everyone born of the Spirit" (John 3:8). After His resurrection He "breathed on" the disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20:22).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4151G
blocks.body:
Greek philosophers, especially the Stoics, spoke of *pneuma* as a fine, fiery substance pervading the universe. Jews thought of God's Spirit as His creative breath (Gen 1:2; Ps 104:30) and as the power that came upon prophets, judges and kings (Judg 3:10; 1 Sam 16:13).

The prophets promised that in the last days God would pour out His Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28) and put His Spirit within His people (Ezek 36:27). At Pentecost, with "a sound like a mighty rushing wind", the apostles said this had come true (Acts 2:2, 16-17).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4151G
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *pneuma* translates Hebrew *ruach*, "wind, breath, spirit" (Gen 1:2, "the Spirit of God was hovering"). In the Hebrew and Greek alike the same word covers all three, so translators must choose.

The Vulgate uses *spiritus*. The KJV mostly says "Holy Ghost" (from Old English *gast*, "spirit"), using "Holy Spirit" only a few times. Modern versions use "Holy Spirit" throughout, since "ghost" now suggests the spirit of a dead person.

blocks.subject: lemma:G4151G
blocks.title: The breath of the Father's family
blocks.body:
The Spirit is the Father's breath and the Son's own Spirit, given to draw us into their shared life. "You have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!" (Rom 8:15). The Spirit's work is not to give us religious experiences detached from Jesus but to unite us to Him and form His life in us (Gal 5:22-23).

The Spirit who hovered over the first creation (Gen 1:2) is renewing creation now, through a people who carry the Father's presence into the world. The breath that raised Jesus from the dead will give life to our mortal bodies too (Rom 8:11).

blocks.subject: lemma:G4151G
blocks.body: Irenaeus described the Son and the Spirit as the two "hands" of God, by which the Father made all things and through which He forms humanity. The Spirit is not a distant force but God Himself at work, shaping humans into the likeness of God. The image keeps the Son and the Spirit together: the Spirit never works apart from the Son, and both carry out the Father's purpose. It became an important picture of the Trinity at work in creation and salvation.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.title: Punishment
blocks.body:
*Kolasis* occurs twice: "these will go away into *kolasis aiōnios*, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matt 25:46), and "fear has to do with *kolasis*, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love" (1 John 4:18). The verb *kolazō* means "to punish" (Acts 4:21; 2 Pet 2:9).

The word's root sense was "pruning, checking", and in some Greek writers it meant corrective punishment. By New Testament times it was often used for punishment in general, including harsh penalties.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.body:
Greek philosophers distinguished kinds of punishment. Aristotle said *kolasis* is inflicted for the sake of the one punished, while *timōria* (vengeance) is for the satisfaction of the one who inflicts it. Plato argued that rational punishment aims to reform or deter rather than to take revenge.

Jewish Greek writings, however, also use *kolasis* for punishments that are clearly retributive or simply severe, including torture (2 Macc 4:38; 4 Macc 8:9). Usage in the period was not uniform.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.body:
The Septuagint and related writings use *kolasis* for God's punishments, sometimes with a disciplining purpose (Wis 16:2, 24) and sometimes simply as penalty (2 Macc 4:38).

The Vulgate rendered Matt 25:46 *supplicium aeternum*, "eternal punishment" (a *supplicium* was often an execution or torment). The KJV said "everlasting punishment", and most modern versions "eternal punishment". A few translations by universalist scholars render it "the chastening of the age" or similar.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.title: Three readings of Matthew 25:46
blocks.body:
**What kind of punishment is *kolasis aiōnios*?**

- *Majority (traditional):* unending retributive punishment, parallel in duration to eternal life (Matt 25:46).
- *Conditional immortality:* a final punishment whose result, destruction, is permanent.
- *Restorative (minority):* drawing on the corrective sense of *kolasis* and the "age" sense of *aiōnios*, some Fathers and modern writers see a purifying judgement that serves God's final restoration.

The lexical evidence is genuinely mixed: *kolasis* can be corrective, but was not always so used. The question is usually settled by wider theology rather than by the word alone.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.body:
**How eternal retribution became the dominant reading.** Augustine argued at length that the punishment of the wicked is unending and that "eternal" in Matt 25:46 must mean the same for punishment and life. Anselm framed sin as an offence against God's infinite honour, which seemed to require infinite satisfaction or punishment. Medieval and Reformation theology generally followed this, understanding hell as the exercise of retributive justice.

Relational readers do not dismiss judgement, but ask whether punishment in God's hands is ever merely retributive, given what Jesus reveals of the Father, and whether 1 John 4:18 sets punishment within the larger work of perfecting love.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.title: Judged by the standard of love
blocks.body:
Matt 25 is a sobering parable: the nations are judged by how they treated "the least of these", in whom the King is hidden (Matt 25:40, 45). Judgement is real, and it is judgement by Jesus' own standard of love.

1 John 4:18 places *kolasis* beside fear and sets both against perfected love. The Father's purpose is not to keep His children afraid of punishment but to perfect them in love. Whatever *kolasis aiōnios* finally means, the Judge is the same Jesus who wept over Jerusalem and prayed for His executioners, and His judgements serve His love, not the other way round.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.body: Gregory of Nyssa taught that God's judgement after death works like a refining fire, painful but purifying, separating evil from the soul so that it can share in God's goodness. He hoped that in the end evil would be wholly removed and even the originator of evil healed. This is a minority view in the church. Gregory was never condemned, and his hope is often distinguished from Origen's.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2851
blocks.body: Origen taught that each sinner kindles his own fire, the torment of conscience, and that God's punishments act like a physician's painful remedies, intended to heal. Later councils condemned aspects of his teaching on the end. His view rests on the conviction that God's anger, as Scripture speaks of it, is not a passion like human rage but a way of describing remedies that serve healing. This reading is a minority position, but it shows that the corrective sense of punishment was alive in the early church, and it remains part of the modern debate.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2920
blocks.title: Judgement and justice
blocks.body:
*Krisis* (47 times) means "judgement, decision", and also "justice". It is the noun of *krinō* (G2919, "to judge, decide", 113 times). It can mean a legal verdict, the act of judging, or the right ordering of things.

In Matt 12:18-20 it renders Hebrew *mishpat* in Isaiah's servant song: the servant will "proclaim justice to the nations ... until He brings justice to victory". In Matt 23:23 Jesus calls "justice, mercy and faithfulness" the weightier matters of the law. John uses it of the crisis Jesus' coming creates: "this is the judgement: the light has come into the world" (John 3:19).

blocks.subject: lemma:G2920
blocks.body:
In Israel, to "judge" meant to govern justly and to rescue the oppressed. The "judges" of the book of Judges were deliverers (Judg 2:16-18). The psalms call creation to rejoice because God "comes to judge the earth" (Ps 96:12-13; 98:9), because His judging means setting things right.

In the Greco-Roman city, *krisis* was the court's decision. Christians lived with both pictures: the judgement seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10) and the righting of the world's wrongs.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2920
blocks.body:
In the Septuagint *krisis* most often renders Hebrew *mishpat*, "justice, judgement, right, custom" (e.g. Isa 42:1-4; Amos 5:24).

The Vulgate used *iudicium*. The KJV used "judgment" almost everywhere, including where "justice" fits better (Matt 12:18; 23:23), and sometimes "damnation" (Matt 23:33, "the damnation of hell"; John 5:29, "the resurrection of damnation"). Modern versions often restore "justice" and "condemnation", which changes the tone markedly.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2920
blocks.body:
**How judgement became mainly condemnation.** In the Latin West, *iudicium* was read through Roman criminal law, and the Last Judgement was pictured chiefly as sentencing. Medieval art and hymnody, such as the *Dies Irae*, made it a day of terror. The KJV's use of "damnation" for *krisis* reinforced this.

The Hebrew background points elsewhere: God's judging is His saving action to set right what is wrong, vindicating the oppressed and ending evil. Relational readers keep the seriousness of judgement but see it as the Father's healing justice, entrusted to the Son.

blocks.subject: lemma:G2920
blocks.title: The Judge is Jesus
blocks.body:
"The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son" (John 5:22). The Judge is Jesus, the one who said "neither do I condemn you" (John 8:11). We need not fear a different verdict from a hidden God.

Jesus also tells us where judgement fell: "Now is the judgement of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out" (John 12:31). At the cross the world's evil and its ruler were judged and defeated. Judgement in Christ is the light exposing darkness in order to heal (John 3:19-21), and justice brought to victory (Matt 12:20).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1347
blocks.title: Justification that brings life
blocks.body:
*Dikaiōsis* means "justification, vindication, the act of putting right". It occurs twice, both in Romans: Jesus "was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our *dikaiōsis*" (Rom 4:25), and "one act of righteousness leads to *dikaiōsis zōēs* for all people", "justification of life" (Rom 5:18).

It is the action noun of *dikaioō*, "to put right" (G1344). In both verses it is tied to resurrection and life.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1347
blocks.body:
In Greek legal usage the word family covered setting a case right, vindication, and the passing of a sentence. Paul places it in Israel's story: Adam's trespass brought condemnation and death to all; Christ's obedience brings justification and life to all (Rom 5:12-21).

Romans 4:25 may echo Isaiah's servant, "delivered up" for sins and making many righteous (Isa 53:11-12).

blocks.subject: lemma:G1347
blocks.body:
The word is rare in the Septuagint, so Paul's usage is shaped mainly by the *dikaioō* family and by Isaiah's servant.

The Vulgate rendered Rom 4:25 *propter iustificationem nostram* and Rom 5:18 *in iustificationem vitae*. The KJV followed: "for our justification" and "unto justification of life". Modern versions vary: "justification and life" (ESV), "justification that brings life" (NIV), "acquittal and life" in some paraphrases.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1347
blocks.body:
**How justification was separated from resurrection.** In much post-Reformation teaching, justification was located chiefly in the cross, as the legal transfer of penalty and righteousness, with the resurrection treated as proof that the payment was accepted. Rom 4:25 was harder to fit into this.

Relational readers note that Paul ties justification directly to Christ's resurrection: we are put right by being joined to the risen One, whose vindication becomes ours.

blocks.subject: lemma:G1347
blocks.title: Raised for our justification
blocks.body:
Justification is not just a cleared record but the gift of life. Jesus was "raised for our justification" (Rom 4:25): when the Father raised Him, He vindicated His Son, and in Him all who belong to Him. Justification is resurrection life shared.

And its scope is breathtaking: "as one trespass led to condemnation for all, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all" (Rom 5:18). The second Adam undoes what the first did. The Father's verdict in Christ over humanity is life.

blocks.subject: lemma:H0430G
blocks.title: God, and the gods
blocks.body:
*Elohim* (about 2,600 times in this sense) is the most common Hebrew word for God. It is plural in form, but when it refers to Israel's God it takes singular verbs: "In the beginning *Elohim* created (singular verb)" (Gen 1:1).

The same word can refer to "gods" of the nations (Exod 20:3), to members of God's heavenly council (Ps 82:1, 6), to the spirit of the dead Samuel (1 Sam 28:13), and possibly to human judges (Exod 21:6, debated). It describes a kind of being, a spiritual being of the unseen world, as well as the one true God.

blocks.subject: lemma:H0430G
blocks.body:
In the Ancient Near East, Canaanite texts from Ugarit speak of *El*, the high god, and of a council of "sons of El". The Hebrew Scriptures use similar language for the LORD's heavenly court: "God stands in the divine council; in the midst of the *elohim* He holds judgement" (Ps 82:1; compare 1 Kgs 22:19; Job 1:6).

Israel's confession was not that no other spiritual beings exist, but that the LORD alone is God Most High, Creator, incomparable among the *elohim* (Exod 15:11; Ps 86:8; 95:3).

blocks.subject: lemma:H0430G
blocks.body:
The Septuagint usually renders *elohim* as *theos*, "God", but in Ps 8:5 it renders "a little lower than *elohim*" as "a little lower than angels", the reading quoted in Heb 2:7. In Ps 82 it kept "gods".

The Vulgate uses *Deus*, and the KJV "God", with "gods", "angels" (Ps 8:5) and "judges" (Exod 21:6; 22:8-9) in some places. Modern versions differ on these debated verses, often noting "God" or "gods" in the margin.

blocks.subject: lemma:H0430G
blocks.title: A plural name for one God

blocks.subject: lemma:H0430G
blocks.title: The God who says 'let us'
blocks.body:
*Elohim* is the Creator who speaks the world into being and calls it good (Gen 1). The New Testament reveals who this God is: the Father, creating through His Word and by His Spirit hovering over the waters (Gen 1:2; John 1:3).

The "let us" of Gen 1:26 has been read by Christians as an echo of the Trinity's shared life. Humanity, male and female, is made in the image of this relational God, to reflect His love and rule over creation. Jesus is the perfect image (Col 1:15) in whom that calling is restored.

blocks.subject: lemma:H0430G
blocks.body: Michael Heiser argued that *elohim* is a term for any being whose proper home is the spiritual world, so the Bible can speak of other *elohim* without denying monotheism. He read Ps 82 and Deut 32:8-9 as showing a divine council, with rebel *elohim* given authority over the nations, a worldview he believed underlies much of the New Testament.

citations.ref: The Unseen Realm (on Psalm 82 and the divine council)

blocks.subject: lemma:H3068G
blocks.title: The divine name
blocks.body:
*YHWH* (about 6,500 times) is the personal name of Israel's God, often called the Tetragrammaton ("four letters"). It is linked with the verb *hayah*, "to be": when Moses asks God's name, God says "I AM WHO I AM" (*ehyeh asher ehyeh*) and then gives the name YHWH (Exod 3:14-15).

The name suggests presence and faithfulness: "I will be with you" (Exod 3:12). Its original pronunciation is uncertain; many scholars reconstruct "Yahweh".

blocks.subject: lemma:H3068G
blocks.body:
Out of reverence, Jews came to avoid pronouncing the name, reading *Adonai*, "my Lord", instead. Scribes wrote the vowels of *Adonai* under the consonants YHWH as a reminder.

The name's character is spelled out when God passes before Moses: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exod 34:6-7). This confession is repeated across the Old Testament (Num 14:18; Ps 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jon 4:2).

blocks.subject: lemma:H3068G
blocks.body:
The Septuagint usually rendered YHWH as *Kyrios*, "Lord", and Exod 3:14 as *egō eimi ho ōn*, "I am the One who is". The Vulgate has *Dominus* and *ego sum qui sum*.

In the late Middle Ages, combining YHWH's consonants with *Adonai*'s vowels produced the hybrid form "Jehovah". Tyndale used it in his Pentateuch (Exod 6:3), and the KJV kept it in a few places (Exod 6:3; Ps 83:18; Isa 12:2; 26:4), elsewhere printing "LORD" in small capitals. Most modern versions follow that convention.

blocks.subject: lemma:H3068G
blocks.title: The name made known in Jesus
blocks.body:
The name YHWH is God's self-giving: He tells His people who He is so they can call on Him. In Exod 34:6 the name is defined as mercy, grace, patience and steadfast love.

Jesus takes up the "I AM" (John 8:58) and says to the Father, "I have made Your name known" (John 17:6, 26). The name revealed at the burning bush is fully revealed in the Son, and the name He teaches us to use is "Father". The early church confessed that Jesus bears the name above every name (Phil 2:9-11), the name of YHWH.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7307G
blocks.title: Wind, breath, spirit
blocks.body:
*Ruach* means "wind, breath, spirit". This sense (216 times) is "spirit"; the database also lists "breath" (H7307H), "temper, mood" and "side, direction" (quarters of the wind).

God's *ruach* hovers over the waters at creation (Gen 1:2), comes upon judges and prophets (Judg 6:34; 1 Sam 10:6), and gives life: "When You send forth Your *ruach*, they are created" (Ps 104:30). It is also the human spirit, the inner life and will (Ps 51:10).

blocks.subject: lemma:H7307G
blocks.body:
In a land dependent on rain and wind, *ruach* was experienced as an invisible, powerful force: the east wind that parted the sea (Exod 14:21) and the scorching wind from the desert (Hos 13:15).

Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones plays on every sense of the word: breath enters the bodies, the four winds blow, and God says "I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live" (Ezek 37:5-14). The prophets looked for a day when God's *ruach* would be poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28-29).

blocks.subject: lemma:H7307G
blocks.body:
The Septuagint usually renders *ruach* as *pneuma*, which carries the same triple sense, and sometimes as *anemos*, "wind". This makes the New Testament's *pneuma* the direct heir of the Hebrew word.

The Vulgate uses *spiritus* and *ventus*. The KJV uses "spirit", "wind" and "breath" according to context, sometimes splitting closely related uses (Gen 1:2 "Spirit"; Gen 8:1 "wind"). Modern versions differ on Gen 1:2, some reading "a mighty wind" or "wind from God".

blocks.subject: lemma:H7307G
blocks.title: Is the Spirit feminine?
blocks.body: *Ruach* is grammatically feminine in most uses. Some writers draw conclusions about a "feminine" side of God or of the Holy Spirit. Others caution that grammatical gender does not indicate personal gender (Greek *pneuma* is neuter and Latin *spiritus* masculine). The point is more often used devotionally than argued from lexical evidence. Scripture does use both maternal and paternal images for God (Isa 66:13; Ps 103:13), so tenderness is not foreign to the Spirit's work, but that point does not depend on grammar.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7307G
blocks.title: The breath of new creation
blocks.body:
The *ruach* of God is the Father's own breath, the life He shares. In Gen 2:7 God breathes life into the first human; in John 20:22 the risen Jesus breathes on His disciples and says "Receive the Holy Spirit". New creation repeats the first creation with the same breath.

The Spirit is not an impersonal force to be harnessed but God present and giving life. Through Jesus the promised outpouring has come, and the dry bones of Israel and the nations live again (Ezek 37; Acts 2:17).

blocks.subject: lemma:H5315G
blocks.title: Throat, life, self
blocks.body:
*Nephesh* (over 750 times across its senses) is usually translated "soul", but its basic meanings are concrete: "throat, neck" (Jon 2:5), "appetite, desire" (Isa 5:14; Prov 23:2), "life" (Gen 9:4-5), "living being" and "person" (Gen 2:7; 46:27), and "self" ("my *nephesh*" often means "I, myself").

Animals are also "living *nephesh*" (Gen 1:20, 24). The man in Gen 2:7 does not *have* a *nephesh*; he *becomes* one when God breathes into dust. The word describes the whole living person, especially in their neediness and desire.

blocks.subject: lemma:H5315G
blocks.body:
Hebrew thought did not divide a human into an immortal soul trapped in a body, as some Greek philosophy did (Plato's *Phaedo*). A person was an animated body, a living whole. The *nephesh* thirsts (Ps 42:1-2), hungers (Deut 12:20) and can be "poured out" in distress (1 Sam 1:15).

"Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your *nephesh* and with all your might" (Deut 6:5) means with your whole life and desire, not only an inner spiritual part.

blocks.subject: lemma:H5315G
blocks.body:
The Septuagint usually renders *nephesh* with *psychē*, which in Greek philosophy often meant the immortal soul. This bridge made it easy for later readers to hear Greek ideas in Hebrew texts.

The Vulgate used *anima*, and the KJV usually "soul", but also "life", "person", "creature", "mind" and "self". Modern versions more often translate by context: "life", "being", "throat", "I", "desire".

blocks.subject: lemma:H5315G
blocks.title: Soul or whole person?
blocks.body: Christians differ on human nature. Some hold that the Bible teaches a soul that survives the body's death (e.g. Matt 10:28; 2 Cor 5:8; Phil 1:23). Others stress that *nephesh* describes the whole person and that hope rests on bodily resurrection, not on an immortal soul. Many hold both: the person continues with God after death, but awaits resurrection. *Nephesh* alone cannot settle the question, but it warns against reading Greek dualism back into Hebrew texts.

blocks.subject: lemma:H5315G
blocks.title: God loves whole people
blocks.body:
*Nephesh* reminds us that God loves embodied people, not disembodied souls. Salvation is not escape from the body but the healing of the whole person. "He restores my *nephesh*" (Ps 23:3): the Shepherd brings back life to the weary self.

Jesus came as a whole human, body and *nephesh*, sharing our thirst, hunger and sorrow ("my soul is very sorrowful", Matt 26:38). He took on our whole humanity so that our whole humanity might be healed and raised.

blocks.subject: lemma:H8451
blocks.title: Instruction
blocks.body:
*Torah* (219 times) means "instruction, teaching, direction". It comes from the verb *yarah*, "to throw, to point out, to teach". A parent's teaching is *torah* (Prov 1:8, "do not forsake your mother's *torah*").

It is used of God's instruction through Moses, especially the covenant laws, and of the first five books of the Bible as a whole. But its primary sense is guidance for life in relationship with God, not a legal code: "The *torah* of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul" (Ps 19:7).

blocks.subject: lemma:H8451
blocks.body:
Ancient Near Eastern law collections, such as the Code of Hammurabi, were issued by kings. Israel's Torah was different in setting: it was given within a covenant after God had rescued His people. "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt" comes before the commandments (Exod 20:2).

In Second Temple Judaism, Torah study became central. The psalmist delights in it day and night (Ps 1:2), and the prophets looked for a time when God would write His Torah on hearts (Jer 31:33) and it would go out from Zion to the nations (Isa 2:3).

blocks.subject: lemma:H8451
blocks.body:
The Septuagint translated *torah* as *nomos*, "law", a word with strong legal and civic associations. Many scholars think this narrowed the sense of "instruction" towards "legislation", though others note that *nomos* could mean custom or way of life too.

The Vulgate followed with *lex*, and Tyndale, the KJV and nearly all English versions say "law". Some Jewish translations prefer "teaching" or "instruction".

blocks.subject: lemma:H8451
blocks.title: The Father's instruction
blocks.body:
Torah was the Father's instruction to children He had already rescued, a gift to shape a family in His likeness. Jesus did not abolish it but fulfilled it (Matt 5:17), showing its heart: love for God and neighbour (Matt 22:37-40).

"The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Jesus is the living Torah, the Word through whom the Father instructs us fully. The written law served as a guardian until Christ came (Gal 3:24); now the Spirit writes God's instruction on our hearts (Jer 31:33; 2 Cor 3:3).

blocks.subject: lemma:H1285
blocks.title: Covenant
blocks.body:
*Berit* (284 times) means "covenant": a binding relationship established by oath, with commitments and often signs. One "cuts" a covenant (*karat berit*), probably from the rite of cutting animals (Gen 15:10, 17-18; Jer 34:18).

God makes covenants with Noah and all creation (Gen 9:9-17), with Abraham (Gen 15; 17), with Israel at Sinai (Exod 24:7-8), and with David (2 Sam 23:5; Ps 89:3). Jeremiah promises a "new covenant" (Jer 31:31-34), which Jesus inaugurates at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).

blocks.subject: lemma:H1285
blocks.body:
Ancient Near Eastern treaties, especially Hittite and Assyrian vassal treaties, offer close parallels: a great king states his past kindness, sets terms, calls witnesses and pronounces blessings and curses. Deuteronomy follows a similar pattern. There were also royal "grants", where a king bound himself to a loyal servant.

In Gen 15 God alone passes between the cut pieces as a smoking fire pot, binding Himself to His promise while Abraham sleeps. Covenant in Scripture is often God's unilateral commitment.

blocks.subject: lemma:H1285
blocks.body:
The Septuagint rendered *berit* not with *synthēkē*, "agreement between equals", but with *diathēkē*, which in ordinary Greek meant a "will" or "testament". This choice stressed that God sets the terms and gives the inheritance. Heb 9:15-17 plays on both senses.

The Vulgate used *foedus*, *pactum* and especially *testamentum*, which gave us "Old Testament" and "New Testament". The KJV says "covenant" in the Old Testament and often "testament" in the New (Matt 26:28; Heb 9:15). Modern versions say "covenant" throughout.

blocks.subject: lemma:H1285
blocks.title: A bond, not a bargain
blocks.body:
A covenant is not a business contract but a bond of belonging: "I will be your God and you shall be my people" (Jer 31:33). Its heart is relationship, often pictured as marriage (Hos 2:19-20) or adoption (2 Sam 7:14).

In Jesus the covenant is fulfilled from both sides. He is God keeping faith with humanity and humanity keeping faith with God. "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20): the Father has bound Himself to us in His Son, unbreakably. We enter by receiving, not by bargaining.

blocks.subject: lemma:H1285
blocks.body: James B. Torrance distinguished a covenant from a contract. A contract is conditional ("if you do this, I will do that"); God's covenant is an unconditional commitment of love that creates obligations of grateful response. He argued that much Western theology, especially "federal" Calvinism, had turned the covenant of grace into a contract. This distinction is a minority view but influential among those who stress God's unconditional grace.

citations.ref: Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace (on covenant and contract)

blocks.subject: lemma:H0530
blocks.title: Steadiness and faithfulness
blocks.body:
*Emunah* (49 times) means "firmness, steadiness, faithfulness, reliability". It comes from the root *aman*, "to be firm", which also gives "Amen". When Moses held up his hands during battle, they were *emunah*, "steady", until sunset (Exod 17:12).

It is used chiefly of God's faithfulness: "great is Your faithfulness" (Lam 3:23; Ps 36:5; 89:1-2) and "a God of faithfulness" (Deut 32:4). It also describes human trustworthiness, as in Hab 2:4, "the righteous shall live by his *emunah*".

blocks.subject: lemma:H0530
blocks.body:
Habakkuk spoke as Babylon threatened Judah (about 600 BC). God's answer was to wait for the vision and live by steady faithfulness through the crisis (Hab 2:2-4).

In Israel, saying "Amen" meant affirming that something was firm and reliable. To have *emunah* towards God was to lean on Him as reliable and to stay loyal to Him.

blocks.subject: lemma:H0530
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *emunah* as *pistis* ("faith, faithfulness") and often as *alētheia*, "truth" (e.g. in the Psalms). In Hab 2:4 it reads "the righteous shall live by *my* faithfulness", God's. Paul quotes Hab 2:4 as "the righteous shall live by faith" (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11).

The Vulgate used *fides* and *veritas*. The KJV has "faithfulness", "truth", "faith" (Hab 2:4) and "steady" (Exod 17:12).

blocks.subject: lemma:H0530
blocks.title: God's steadiness first
blocks.body:
Biblical faith starts with God's faithfulness, not ours. "If we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself" (2 Tim 2:13). Our trust is a response to His reliability.

Jesus is God's *emunah* in person: the faithful Son who kept trusting the Father through the cross, and the "Amen" of God's promises (2 Cor 1:20; Rev 3:14). Living by faith is leaning our whole weight on Him, steadied like Moses' hands, held up by others when we tire.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7725G
blocks.title: To turn back home
blocks.body:
*Shuv* is one of the most common verbs in the Hebrew Bible (over 1,000 uses across its senses). It means "to turn, return, turn back, restore". This sense ("return", 628 times) covers going back to a place or a person; the database also separates senses like "repent", "rescue", "turn back", "repay" and "reply".

Spiritually, it is the main Old Testament word for repentance: returning to God (Hos 14:1; Joel 2:12-13). It is also used of God turning back to His people: "Return to me, and I will return to you" (Zech 1:3).

blocks.subject: lemma:H7725G
blocks.body:
*Shuv* is the language of exile and homecoming. Israel was sent into exile for unfaithfulness, and the prophets promised that God would "restore the fortunes" (*shuv shevut*) of His people and bring them home (Jer 29:14; 30:3).

The book of Ruth uses *shuv* repeatedly as Naomi and Ruth return from Moab to Bethlehem (Ruth 1). In later Jewish tradition *teshuvah*, "return", became the standard word for repentance.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7725G
blocks.body:
The Septuagint usually renders *shuv* with *epistrephō*, "to turn, return", or *apostrephō*. The New Testament's *metanoeō*, "repent", corresponds more closely to Hebrew *nicham*, but carries *shuv*'s sense of turning back to God.

The Vulgate uses *convertere* and *reverti*, which gave English "convert". The KJV uses "turn", "return", "restore" and "convert" ("converting the soul", Ps 19:7). Modern versions often use "restore" or "repent".

blocks.subject: lemma:H7725G
blocks.title: Homecoming
blocks.body:
Repentance in the Old Testament is a homecoming, not a penance. "Return, faithless Israel ... for I am merciful" (Jer 3:12). God Himself provides the turning: "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored" (Lam 5:21). He "restores my soul" (Ps 23:3).

Jesus' parable of the lost son is *shuv* in story form: the son turns home, and the father is already watching the road (Luke 15:17-20). And in Christ, God has "returned" to His people in person, bringing the exile to its true end.

blocks.subject: lemma:H1350A
blocks.title: Kinsman-redeemer
blocks.body:
*Ga'al* (88 times in this sense) means "to redeem, to act as kinsman". Its participle *go'el* is the "kinsman-redeemer": the nearest relative responsible for a family member in trouble. He bought back land sold in poverty (Lev 25:25), freed a relative sold into slavery (Lev 25:47-49), married a childless widow to keep the family name (Ruth 4), and as "avenger of blood" pursued a murderer (Num 35:19).

God calls Himself Israel's *Go'el*: "Fear not ... I am your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel" (Isa 41:14; 43:14; 44:6).

blocks.subject: lemma:H1350A
blocks.body:
In a tribal society, the extended family was the safety net. The *go'el* had both the right and the duty to rescue a relative, because the relative's loss was the family's loss.

Ruth shows it in action. Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband, redeems the family land and marries Ruth, a Moabite widow (Ruth 3:9-13; 4:1-10). Their son becomes grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17). Job, in his suffering, cries "I know that my *go'el* lives" (Job 19:25).

blocks.subject: lemma:H1350A
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *ga'al* mostly as *lytroō*, "to redeem, ransom", and sometimes *rhyomai*, "to deliver" (Isa 59:20, quoted in Rom 11:26: "the Deliverer will come from Zion"). In Ruth and Numbers it uses *anchisteus*, "next of kin".

The Vulgate uses *redimere* and *redemptor* (Job 19:25, *scio quod redemptor meus vivit*) and *propinquus*, "kinsman". The KJV says "redeemer", "kinsman" and "avenger of the blood". Modern versions keep these, often with "guardian-redeemer" in Ruth.

blocks.subject: lemma:H1350A
blocks.title: Our nearest relative
blocks.body:
Redemption in Hebrew is family language. A *go'el* redeems because he is kin. That is why the Son became flesh: "Since the children share in flesh and blood, He Himself likewise partook of the same ... He is not ashamed to call them brothers" (Heb 2:11-14).

God is not buying strangers from a market; He is acting as our nearest relative, rescuing His own. Isaiah links the titles: "You, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is Your name" (Isa 63:16). Redemption is the Father's family loyalty, carried out by the Son, our kinsman.

blocks.subject: lemma:H1350A
blocks.body: T. F. Torrance analysed Old Testament redemption through three Hebrew terms: *padah* (redemption by mighty act), *kipper* (atoning cleansing) and *ga'al* (redemption by a kinsman). He held that *go'el* points to Christ's redeeming through His personal kinship with us in the incarnation, not as an outside agent. This kinship emphasis fits Heb 2:11-17, which grounds Christ's saving work in His sharing our flesh and blood.

citations.ref: Atonement: The Person and Work of Christ (on padah, kipper and go'el)

blocks.subject: lemma:H0160
blocks.title: Love
blocks.body:
*Ahavah* (38 times) is the noun "love", from the verb *ahav*, "to love" (H0157). It describes human love, Jacob's seven years for Rachel seemed "but a few days because of his *ahavah* for her" (Gen 29:20), friendship (1 Sam 18:3; 2 Sam 1:26) and God's love for His people.

"I have loved you with an everlasting *ahavah*" (Jer 31:3); "I led them with cords of kindness, with bands of *ahavah*" (Hos 11:4); "He will quiet you by His love; He will rejoice over you with singing" (Zeph 3:17).

blocks.subject: lemma:H0160
blocks.body:
In Ancient Near Eastern treaties "love" could describe the loyalty a vassal owed his overlord. Deuteronomy's command to "love the LORD your God" (Deut 6:5) carries this covenant loyalty, but goes beyond it: God's love for Israel is personal and unearned, "not because you were more in number ... but because the LORD loves you" (Deut 7:7-8).

The Song of Songs celebrates human love as "strong as death ... many waters cannot quench love" (Song 8:6-7).

blocks.subject: lemma:H0160
blocks.body:
The Septuagint usually renders *ahavah* with *agapē*, a noun barely used in Greek before. This choice made *agapē* available to the New Testament writers as their main word for love.

The Vulgate used *dilectio* and *caritas* (Song 8:6, *fortis est ut mors dilectio*). Tyndale, the KJV and modern versions say "love". The Hebrew *ahavah* therefore stands directly behind the New Testament's great statements about love, such as 1 Cor 13 and 1 John 4.

blocks.subject: lemma:H0160
blocks.title: Love that chooses
blocks.body:
God's love is not drawn out by our attractiveness; it is His free choice and His nature. "The LORD set His love on you ... because the LORD loves you" (Deut 7:7-8): the reason is love itself.

Hosea pictures God as a parent teaching a toddler to walk, lifting the child to his cheek (Hos 11:1-4). That is the Father Jesus reveals. "God is love" (1 John 4:8) is not a new idea in the New Testament but the full unveiling of the *ahavah* Israel had glimpsed, now embodied in the Son.

blocks.subject: lemma:H3519
blocks.title: Weight and glory
blocks.body:
*Kavod* (200 times) comes from a root meaning "to be heavy". It means "weight, substance", then "wealth" (Gen 31:1), "honour, dignity" (Ps 3:3) and "glory". To "honour" father and mother is to give them weight (Exod 20:12, the related verb).

God's *kavod* is His manifest presence, often as cloud and fire: it settles on Sinai (Exod 24:16-17), fills the tabernacle (Exod 40:34-35) and the temple (1 Kgs 8:11). "The whole earth is full of His *kavod*" (Isa 6:3).

blocks.subject: lemma:H3519
blocks.body:
In an honour-shame culture, *kavod* was reputation and social weight. People sought it; the poor and the shamed lacked it.

Israel's history traces God's glory: present in the tabernacle and temple, departing in judgement. When the ark was captured, a newborn was named Ichabod, "the glory has departed" (1 Sam 4:21-22). Ezekiel saw the glory leave the temple before the exile (Ezek 10:18-19) and return in a vision of restoration (Ezek 43:2-5).

blocks.subject: lemma:H3519
blocks.body:
The Septuagint translated *kavod* as *doxa*, transforming the Greek word from "opinion, reputation" into "radiant glory". This is how *doxa* came to carry the meaning it has in the New Testament.

The Vulgate uses *gloria* and *honor*, and the KJV "glory", "honour" and occasionally "riches". Modern versions follow similarly. Some English versions also render the related verb as "honour", as in the command to honour father and mother (Exod 20:12), which hides the link with "glory". Seeing the connection shows that giving glory is giving weight.

blocks.subject: lemma:H3519
blocks.title: Glory returning
blocks.body:
When Moses asked to see God's glory, God showed His goodness and proclaimed His name of mercy (Exod 33:18-19; 34:6). God's weightiest reality is His love.

The glory that left the temple returned in Jesus: "the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us, and we beheld His glory" (John 1:14). And it is spreading: "the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea" (Hab 2:14). That promise grounds a postmillennial hope: the Father's glory, seen in the face of Christ, will fill the earth.

blocks.subject: lemma:H2398
blocks.title: To miss, to sin, to cleanse
blocks.body:
*Chata* (238 times) means "to miss, to fail, to sin". Its concrete sense appears in Judg 20:16: slingers who could hit a hair "and not miss". Prov 19:2 speaks of one who hurries and "misses the way".

Most often it means sinning against God or another person: "Against You, You only, have I sinned" (Ps 51:4); "How can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" (Gen 39:9). Intensive forms mean the opposite: "to purify, de-sin", as in "purge me with hyssop" (Ps 51:7) and cleansing rites (Num 19:12). The noun *chatta't* means both "sin" and "sin offering" (Lev 4).

blocks.subject: lemma:H2398
blocks.body:
In Israel's covenant setting, sin was failure of loyalty and breach of relationship, with God and with neighbour. It defiled people and the sanctuary, which needed cleansing through the *chatta't* offering and the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:16).

Sin could be expressed as debt: when Judah offers himself for Benjamin, he says "I will bear the blame (*chata'ti*) before my father all my life" (Gen 43:9). Later Aramaic used the word for "debt" for sin, which is why the Lord's Prayer says "forgive us our debts" (Matt 6:12).

blocks.subject: lemma:H2398
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *chata* with *hamartanō*, "to sin, err", and *chatta't* with *hamartia*, sometimes in the sense "sin offering" (Lev 4:24).

The Vulgate uses *peccare*, and the KJV "sin", with "offend" (Gen 20:9), "miss" (Judg 20:16) and "purify" or "cleanse" for the intensive forms. Modern versions follow similarly. Because English "sin" has no cleansing counterpart, the double sense of the Hebrew root is mostly lost in translation.

blocks.subject: lemma:H2398
blocks.body:
**How sin became chiefly an offence against honour and law.** Anselm defined sin as failing to give God the honour due to Him, an offence requiring satisfaction. Later Protestant theology framed sin as transgression of God's law, incurring guilt and penalty under divine justice.

The Hebrew vocabulary is broader: sin is missing the way, breaking faith, defiling what is holy. Relational readers keep sin's seriousness but locate it in broken relationship and its cure in cleansing and restoration, as the intensive "de-sin" forms of *chata* suggest.

blocks.subject: lemma:H2398
blocks.title: Missing the way, made clean
blocks.body:
Sin misses the life the Father intends. It wounds relationships: David's sin against Uriah was sin against God (2 Sam 12:13; Ps 51:4). The same Hebrew root also speaks of cleansing: the God who is sinned against is the God who "un-sins" us (Ps 51:7).

That is the shape of Jesus' ministry. He touches the unclean and cleanses them, forgives sinners and restores them to the table. "He was manifested to take away sins" (1 John 3:5). Sin is not the last word; the Father's cleansing love is.

blocks.subject: lemma:H4941G
blocks.title: Justice that sets right
blocks.body:
*Mishpat* (over 400 times across its senses) means "justice, judgement, right, ordinance, custom". It comes from *shaphat*, "to judge, govern, set right". This sense ("judgement", 216 times) covers court decisions and God's acts of judgement; the database separates "justice", "custom" and "rule".

*Mishpat* is what the judge does to put wrongs right, especially for the vulnerable: God "executes *mishpat* for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner" (Deut 10:18). It is often paired with *tsedaqah*, "righteousness" (Amos 5:24; Ps 89:14).

blocks.subject: lemma:H4941G
blocks.body:
Ancient Near Eastern kings claimed to establish justice for the weak; Hammurabi's prologue says his laws were given so that the strong might not oppress the weak. Israel's prophets held their kings to that standard and found them wanting: a true king "judged the cause of the poor and needy ... Is not this to know me? declares the LORD" (Jer 22:16).

Abraham appeals to God on this basis: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do *mishpat*?" (Gen 18:25).

blocks.subject: lemma:H4941G
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *mishpat* with *krisis* (judgement, justice), *krima* (verdict) and *dikaiōma* (ordinance). Matthew's quotation of Isa 42 uses *krisis* for *mishpat* (Matt 12:18-20).

The Vulgate used *iudicium*. The KJV usually says "judgment", "Let judgment run down as waters" (Amos 5:24), "to do justly" (Mic 6:8); modern versions say "justice" far more often, which brings out its social and saving sense.

blocks.subject: lemma:H4941G
blocks.body:
**How justice became retribution.** When *mishpat* became Latin *iudicium* and was read through Roman criminal law, God's justice came to be understood mainly as giving each person the punishment they deserve. Medieval and Reformation theology often defined divine justice as retributive: sin must be punished for justice to be satisfied.

The Hebrew prophets more often picture *mishpat* as God's action to rescue the oppressed and restore what is broken (Isa 1:17; Ps 146:7). Relational readers therefore speak of restorative justice: God's judgement aims to make things right, not merely to balance the scales.

blocks.subject: lemma:H4941G
blocks.title: Justice that heals
blocks.body:
"He has told you, O man, what is good: to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God" (Mic 6:8). God's justice and mercy are not opposites to be reconciled; they work together to restore.

Jesus is the servant who "will bring forth justice to the nations ... a bruised reed He will not break" (Isa 42:1-3; Matt 12:18-20). His justice is gentle and unstoppable, healing the bruised. The Father's justice looks like Jesus at the table with outcasts and on the cross forgiving enemies, setting the world right by love.

blocks.subject: lemma:H4941G
blocks.body: Darrin Snyder Belousek argues that biblical justice is fundamentally covenantal and restorative: God's justice is His faithfulness to set right what is wrong, vindicate the oppressed and restore relationship, rather than a principle requiring retribution. He applies this to the meaning of the cross. His work draws together Old Testament *mishpat*, the prophets and Paul, and it is often cited by those who favour restorative justice in criminal law and church practice as well as in theology. Many evangelical scholars still defend a retributive reading.
