blocks.subject: lemma:H7356B
blocks.title: Womb-love
blocks.body:
*Rachamim* (39 times) means "compassion, tender mercy". It is the plural of *rechem*, "womb" (H7356A), so the word suggests womb-love, the visceral tenderness of a mother for her child. The verb *racham* (H7355) means "to have compassion", and the adjective *rachum* describes God as "merciful" (Exod 34:6).

"Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion (*racham*) on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you" (Isa 49:15).

blocks.subject: lemma:H7356B
blocks.body:
Ancient people located deep feeling in the body. When Joseph saw his brother Benjamin, "his compassion (*rachamim*) grew warm" and he left to weep (Gen 43:30). The true mother before Solomon was moved because her *rachamim* "yearned" for her son (1 Kgs 3:26).

Hosea names his daughter Lo-Ruhamah, "No Mercy", as a sign of judgement, then promises "I will have mercy on No Mercy" (Hos 1:6; 2:23), a promise Paul applies to the Gentiles (Rom 9:25).

blocks.subject: lemma:H7356B
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *rachamim* with *oiktirmos*, "pity, mercy", and *eleos*, "mercy". Later Greek used *splanchna*, "inward parts", for the same feeling, the background of Jesus' *splanchnizomai* (Luke 15:20).

The Vulgate uses *misericordia*, *miserationes* and *viscera*. The KJV renders "tender mercies" (Ps 51:1; 103:4), "compassion", and in places "bowels" (Gen 43:30, "his bowels did yearn upon his brother"). Modern versions say "compassion" or "mercy", losing the physical image.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7356B
blocks.title: The yearning of God
blocks.body:
God's compassion is felt, not merely decided. "Is Ephraim my dear son? ... my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him" (Jer 31:20). "As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion" (Ps 103:13). Scripture uses both mother and father images to say the same thing.

Jesus is this womb-love in flesh. When the father in His parable sees his son, he is "moved with compassion" and runs (Luke 15:20). "His compassions never fail; they are new every morning" (Lam 3:22-23).

blocks.subject: lemma:H2896A
blocks.title: Good
blocks.body:
*Tov* (384 times in this sense, the adjective) means "good, pleasant, beautiful, beneficial, right". It describes what is pleasing to the senses (Gen 2:9), useful, kind (Ps 145:9), morally right (Mic 6:8) and well-made (Exod 2:2, the baby Moses was "a fine child").

In Gen 1 God sees each part of creation and calls it *tov*, and after making humanity, "very good" (Gen 1:31). The first "not good" in Scripture is loneliness: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Gen 2:18).

blocks.subject: lemma:H2896A
blocks.body:
Ancient Near Eastern creation stories, such as the Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, picture the world made from conflict among gods, with humans created to do the gods' labour. Genesis presents creation as the unopposed, good work of one God who blesses humanity and gives it rest.

Israel's worship refrain was "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His steadfast love endures for ever" (Ps 106:1; 107:1; 118:1; 136:1).

blocks.subject: lemma:H2896A
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *tov* in Gen 1 as *kalos*, "good, beautiful, fitting", and elsewhere often as *agathos*, "good". In Ps 34:8, "taste and see that the LORD is good", it uses *chrēstos*, "kind", which 1 Pet 2:3 quotes.

The Vulgate uses *bonus*, and the KJV and modern versions "good", with "pleasant", "fair", "better" and "well" according to context.

blocks.subject: lemma:H2896A
blocks.title: A creation God delights in
blocks.body:
Creation begins with God's delight. Before the fall, the first word over the world and over humanity is "good" and "very good" (Gen 1:31). The Father is not a reluctant creator but a generous one, and the first lack is the absence of communion (Gen 2:18).

Jesus said "No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18), and then showed what that goodness looks like: healing, feeding, forgiving. Because God is good, His judgements and His mercy serve the same end, the restoration of a creation He has never stopped calling good. "The LORD is good to all, and His mercy is over all that He has made" (Ps 145:9).

blocks.subject: lemma:H2896A
blocks.body: Athanasius taught that God, being good and the source of goodness, does not begrudge existence to anything, and so made all things out of nothing through His Word. Because He made humanity in goodness, He could not allow His work to perish through corruption; His goodness is the reason for the Incarnation. This grounds salvation in God's goodness rather than in His offended honour.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7585
blocks.title: The realm of the dead
blocks.body:
*She'ol* (66 times) is the realm of the dead, pictured as deep beneath the earth. All the dead go there, righteous and wicked alike: Jacob expects to go down to Sheol mourning his son (Gen 37:35). It is a place of silence and darkness: "in Sheol who will give You praise?" (Ps 6:5; 88:10-12).

Yet it is not beyond God: "If I make my bed in Sheol, You are there" (Ps 139:8); "the LORD brings down to Sheol and raises up" (1 Sam 2:6). Its etymology is uncertain.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7585
blocks.body:
Neighbouring cultures had their own underworlds, such as the Mesopotamian "land of no return" and the Canaanite god Mot (Death), who swallowed his victims. Sheol is often pictured as a hungry mouth: "Sheol has enlarged its appetite" (Isa 5:14; Prov 27:20).

Within the Old Testament, hope begins to break through Sheol's gloom: "God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol" (Ps 49:15); "You will not abandon my soul to Sheol" (Ps 16:10). Later, Daniel speaks clearly of resurrection (Dan 12:2).

blocks.subject: lemma:H7585
blocks.body:
The Septuagint renders *she'ol* almost always as *hadēs*, which carried the term into the New Testament (Ps 16:10 in Acts 2:27).

The Vulgate used *infernus* and *inferi*. The KJV translated *she'ol* as "hell" 31 times, "grave" 31 times and "pit" 3 times, so English readers often could not see it was one word, and "hell" read in later senses of punishment. Most modern versions keep "Sheol" or use "grave" or "realm of the dead".

blocks.subject: lemma:H7585
blocks.title: How Israel's hope grew
blocks.body: Scholars debate how Israel's view of death developed: whether Sheol was originally simply the grave or the shadowy existence of the dead, and how and when belief in resurrection and in distinct destinies for righteous and wicked emerged (Dan 12:2; later 1 Enoch 22). Christians also differ on whether Sheol had divisions before Christ's resurrection, a view drawn from Luke 16:22-26.

blocks.subject: lemma:H7585
blocks.title: Christ in the depths
blocks.body:
Sheol is the end of the road for all of Adam's children, and God refuses to leave it that way. "Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? ... O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?" (Hos 13:14). Paul hears that as a cry of victory fulfilled in Christ's resurrection (1 Cor 15:55).

Jesus went down where we go. He was not abandoned to Sheol (Acts 2:27, 31), and He now holds its keys (Rev 1:18). Even in the deepest place, "You are there" (Ps 139:8), and in Christ that presence has become rescue.
